principles.text: Aim for modest, self-funded success that makes you happy rather than the VC-backed big-exit story the tech press sells.
principles.quote: I’m all about figuring out what’s going to make a person happy and then going after that with ravenous determination, instead of pursuing what we’re told is going to make us happy by the tech press

principles.text: SEO is an unsexy but powerful channel; it can deliver targeted, high-converting traffic with ROI beating most other sources.
principles.quote: People don’t tend to talk about SEO as a sexy marketing approach, but it can generate enormous amounts of highly-targeted, high-converting traffic.

principles.text: Find acquisition targets among neglected products you already know; cold email the owner directly.
principles.quote: On a warm day in early June I cold emailed the owner through the website contact form.

principles.text: Anchor on your own valuation from experience rehabbing apps; don't pay "dot com" pricing when the owner counters high.
principles.quote: I’ve acquired many web apps in the past, and I wasn’t prepared to pay “dot com” pricing for it.

principles.text: After buying, fix infrastructure risk first, then plug funnel leaks like unended trials, missing trial emails and dead-end content pages.
principles.quote: During the trial period a user received exactly zero emails. No reminders to check out their fancy new suggestions. No inquiry as to why they never installed the code. Zip.

principles.text: Use contractors rather than employees to rebuild a product quickly, and pitch in on the code yourself.
principles.quote: And that something involved me hiring a developer and a designer to help me revamp this thing (both contractors, of course, since I don't hire employees). I also put in quite a bit of coding time myself.

sources.title: Rob Walling: The 5 stages of product-market fit and why it's not binary
sources.originalTitle: The 5 stages of product market fit
sources.summary: Rob argues product-market fit is a spectrum, not a light switch. He lays out five stages (pre, weak, emerging, strong, mature) with typical MRR, churn and growth ranges, and the focus areas and pitfalls at each. The goal is to know your stage and do that stage's work.

principles.text: PMF is a spectrum. Ask what stage you're in and what to focus on, not whether you have it.
principles.quote: The question isn't "do I have PMF?" The better question is: "what stage am I in, and what should I focus on to strengthen it?"

principles.text: Pre-PMF, don't scale marketing. Make sure you're building something people actually want.
principles.quote: If you're pre-PMF, don't worry about scaling marketing. Worry about whether you're building something people actually want.

principles.text: A big audience or strong marketing can pile up customers without real PMF. Retention is the true signal.
principles.quote: If churn is 10% or higher per month, you're effectively pre-PMF regardless of your other metrics.

principles.text: Big annual contracts can mask PMF problems. Watch retention and expansion, not just revenue.
principles.quote: A few $100K contracts can mask underlying PMF problems. Pay attention to retention and expansion, not just revenue.

principles.text: At emerging PMF, resist enterprise distractions. Find repeatable channels and strengthen retention.
principles.quote: If you're at emerging PMF, don't get distracted by enterprise sales. Focus on finding repeatable channels and strengthening retention.

principles.text: At strong PMF, stop doing everything yourself. Hire and build a team to reach the next stage.
principles.quote: If you're at strong PMF, don't keep doing everything yourself. Hire and build the team that can take you to the next stage.

sources.title: Rob Walling's 1-9-90 rule: why most startups should never raise venture capital
sources.originalTitle: 90% of Startups Should Never Raise Venture Capital
sources.summary: A write-up of a Way of Product conversation with Rob Walling. He argues that about 1% of software startups should consider VC, 9% other funding, and 90% should bootstrap. He cites Drip and boring B2B SaaS niches as proof that great businesses don't need venture money.

principles.text: The belief that every startup must raise funding is a false narrative; bootstrapping is a legitimate default.
principles.quote: that everybody who does a startup has to raise funding. It’s just not true.

principles.text: Even experienced founders absorb the venture story; question it rather than assume it applies to you.
principles.quote: The venture industrial complex has brainwashed us all. Me included, back in the early 2000s.

principles.text: Boring, niche B2B SaaS can be a great business; look at unglamorous niches rather than headline-grabbing ideas.
principles.quote: there’s like boring B2B SaaS businesses that I’ve invested in. And it just gives you an idea of the types of things, the niches you can be in.

principles.text: Success comes from spotting an underserved gap in the market; luck only multiplies it.
principles.quote: It wasn’t luck. I also happened to see the gap.

principles.text: A merely great, profitable business is a worthy outcome even without outsized scale or luck.
principles.quote: It’d still be a great fucking business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling argues the cost of launching a SaaS is now near zero for building, and the real expense is distribution. He walks through free tooling, three ways to get a product built, low-budget channels (one fast, one slow), and why keeping your day job and learning to spot problems matter most.

chunks.heading: Real cost of starting a SaaS from $0: marketing and distribution, not building
chunks.text:
- Rob says first-time founders overestimate what the product costs to build and underestimate what it costs to get anyone to care.
- The real expense, in time or money, is finding people who will pay. He calls this marketing, sales or "distribution".
- He says that without a paying customer "you actually have a hobby, not a business."
- He says "Revenue validates the business, everything else is theater."
- In applications to Tiny Seed, his B2B SaaS accelerator, he sees founders spend 6 months perfecting the product and setting up bank accounts, with zero customer conversations.
- He says founders pick easy tasks over complex, uncertain ones such as customer conversations.
- He says the money needed to get a SaaS off the ground has never been lower.

chunks.heading: Skip the formalities and use free or cheap tools until revenue arrives
chunks.text:
- Rob says he could cross about 80% of the expense list off. Before revenue, don't form an LLC, set up a bank account, order business cards or obsess over a logo.
- He ran a US sole proprietorship for five or six years. He made six figures of revenue as a consultant and through products without an LLC.
- He gives this as his own experience, not legal advice. Most people formalize a corporate entity after they have real revenue.
- Payments: Stripe is free to set up, and you pay only when you get paid.
- Education is free or cheap:
  - His podcast Startups for the Rest of Us has more than 830 weekly episodes, recorded 52 a year since 2010.
  - YouTube, free book chapters online and the MicroConf community on Twitter.
  - Most of his books are about $10 on Kindle, PDF or audio.
- Hosting: Vercel and Supabase have free tiers, and AWS and Google Cloud offer startup credits. An MVP typically runs well under $50 a month.
- AI coding tools have free tiers or cost about $20 a month. Domains are about $10-15 a year.
- Total hard-dollar cost for a functional MVP can be under $100 if the founder does a lot themselves.
- He says the barrier is not money but "knowing where to focus."

chunks.heading: Three ways to get a product built (best to worst)
chunks.text:
**Option A: build it yourself, if you can code.**
- This is his preferred path. Build nights and weekends around a day job or consulting.
- With AI assistants like Cursor and Claude Code, weekend tasks now take an evening. Shipping an MVP in under 4 weeks of nights and weekends is realistic.
- The fundamentals are unchanged:
  - Find the core use case.
  - Shrink scope ruthlessly.
  - Ship, then iterate on real feedback rather than guesswork.
- Building faster doesn't remove the need to get prospects using the product. The odds of building the right thing from your own head are "very, very low."
- The advantage is that you can maintain and extend the product yourself. "Product is never done," and it isn't a one-time agency job.

**Option B: non-developer using AI-assisted or no-code tools.**
- Tools named: Cursor, Claude Code, Lovable, Bolt and Replit.
- Works well for prototypes, simple CRUD apps, landing pages with functionality, internal tools and MVPs for customer feedback.
- Gets hard with complex business logic, deep integrations, ongoing maintenance and scaling. Code becomes difficult to modify at the edges.
- Recommended workflow:
  1. Build a prototype with AI tools.
  2. Validate willingness to pay.
  3. Learn to maintain it yourself, or hire a developer once there is revenue.
- Two Tiny Seed-funded companies built a no-code product to validate it, then hired a developer to rewrite it in full code.
- Cost is $0-20 a month, maybe $100 on pricier tiers. The real investment is time.

**Option C: find a technical co-founder.**
- "I have the idea" is not enough, especially now that non-technical people can build prototypes.
- The non-technical founder owns everything but the code: customer conversations, demos, sales, landing pages and marketing.
- The best pairings come from shared context, such as the same industry, meeting at MicroConf or the same community. He has not seen many work out from a Reddit post.
- The best pairings are complementary. Two-developer teams often both want to write code and nobody sells.
- One co-founder must head up driving demand and building a marketing and sales engine.

chunks.heading: Marketing with no budget: pair a fast channel with a slow one
chunks.text:
- With no budget, paid ads are off the table and time is the main resource.
- Slow, compounding channels:
  - SEO and content can take months to pay off but compound.
  - SEO isn't just Google. It includes YouTube (the number two search engine), app stores such as the WordPress and Shopify stores, Reddit, niche directories, and AI answer engines like ChatGPT and Perplexity.
  - All of these reward useful content that answers real questions.
  - An SEO engine that ranks in Google brings organic traffic month after month.
- Fast channels:
  - Cold outreach is free and fast. It depends on a signal, "an external cue" showing someone needs your product "now, not someday." Without a signal it is spam.
  - Partnerships and integrations: co-promote with complementary products. They cost time, but leads can last for years.
  - Communities and events: meetups, Slack groups, subreddits, Facebook groups and Discord where your vertical gathers. Show up and be genuinely helpful. This reaches early customers and can be a long-term channel.
- His ideal plan is one fast channel (outreach or communities) and one slow channel (SEO or content), worked at the same time.
  - Fast only means always chasing the next lead.
  - Slow only means starving for 3, 6 or 9 months while waiting.

chunks.heading: Using AI for content without sounding generic
chunks.text:
- AI lets everyone produce more faster, so it isn't an edge. What stands out is original thinking, proprietary data and real expertise.
- He says "A thousand AI blog posts are probably not going to beat one piece from someone who knows the problem."
- At MicroConf and Tiny Seed, AI helps with prep, but the script is not AI-generated. This video was outlined with AI assistance.
- The team feeds its own internal knowledge, original thinking and frameworks into AI, which then fleshes out the edges.
- Asking AI to outline a video from a title alone gives something "bland," "generic" and "the average."

chunks.heading: Keep your day job and build nights and weekends
chunks.text:
- For the first year or longer, the founder is the entire company: sales, support, engineering and marketing.
- The default path, and the way he and most successful bootstrap founders did it, is to keep the day job until the business replaces it or gets close.
- He says posts on X and Reddit from people who quit, ran out of runway and had to get a job again are a pattern to avoid.
- Exceptions are founders with savings or a supportive partner or spouse.
- Benefits of the paycheck:
  - It removes the ticking-clock pressure.
  - It allows patience, better decisions, less desperation and longer-term bets.
- Timeline is unpredictable: maybe 3 months, 6 months or 18 months.
- A finite cash reserve pushes founders into short-term decisions. He calls a steady paycheck "an underrated competitive advantage."

chunks.heading: Hard work, luck and skill, and finding problems worth solving
chunks.text:
- Every successful startup he knows combines hard work, luck and skill in different proportions. This includes his own, the 230+ he has invested in and thousands he has watched through MicroConf and Startups for the Rest of Us.
- Luck can't be controlled, but how much the outcome depends on it can be.
- Hard work is necessary but not sufficient. Plenty of founders grind on the wrong things for years.
- Skill directs the work: marketing, product sense, hearing what customers say, knowing what to build and how to get it into people's hands.
- The goal is to minimize luck's role by building skills systematically and putting in the work.
- The most important early skill is spotting problems worth solving. Ideas usually come from paying attention, not a flash of inspiration, especially at a day job where you see broken workflows and manual processes.
- He offers a free ebook, "the 9-to-5 audit", a structured framework for finding SaaS ideas at work, at robwalling.com/ideas.
- He says none of the above matters if you build the wrong thing, and finding the idea is hard.
- He surveyed more than 200 successful SaaS founders on where they found their idea and covers eight methods in a follow-up video.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob explains how to prioritize B2B SaaS content using the five stages of customer awareness (unaware, problem, solution, product, most aware). He covers three ways to place a prospect in a stage and gives SaaS examples per stage, advising founders to start at the bottom of the funnel and work upward.

chunks.heading: Rob's framework: five stages of customer awareness applied to B2B content
chunks.text:
- Rob built this after a Tiny Seed founder in 2023 wrote down 15 blog post ideas and then panicked: "how do I prioritize any of this?" Rob realized there was no framework for it.
- He takes Eugene Schwartz's five stages of awareness (1950s-60s, written for consumer ads) and applies them to B2B content. Most prior art he found was B2C.
- He says this applies even to founders who do only outbound sales. The last two stages need content (case studies, versus pages, demos) even if it is "sales literature" and not marketing.
- Rob's rule of thumb: if you have nothing, start at the bottom (most aware) and work backwards up the funnel.

The five stages, with his email-marketing-for-realtors example:
1. **Unaware**: the prospect doesn't know they have a problem (a realtor doesn't know they need more leads). In B2B this is the hardest and "you really kind of don't want to be there". It means cold outreach plus education, or inventing a category.
2. **Problem aware**: they know the problem but not the solutions. They search "how do I send bulk email" or "email marketing templates", not product names.
3. **Solution aware**: they know the category but not specific products. They search "best email marketing software".
4. **Product aware**: they know your product and compare it with competitors (MailChimp vs Klaviyo, ActiveCampaign vs Drip).
5. **Most aware**: educated on the market and close to buying, or already bought and telling peers.

His B2C illustration: running shoes. Prime Day reminded him he needed shoes, then he searched "best running shoes", then compared model numbers (Nike Streak Fly vs ASICS GT-2000), then searched "buy ASICS GT-2000" and "cheapest".

chunks.heading: Three ways to tell which stage a prospect is in
chunks.text:
Rob says attribution is never 100%. If you get to 75-80% attribution of where customers come from, "you're doing pretty well", and this is harder now that Google withholds keywords ("keyword not provided"). The methods below are "good enough".

1. **Ask on sales calls** (high-touch):
   - When do you plan to buy?
   - Are you comparing us to other products, and which ones?
   - Buying soon, or comparing us to MailChimp and Klaviyo, means roughly stage 4-5. Early research with no other vendors considered means roughly stage 2-3.
   - If he were running SaaS sales today, Rob would add a guessed awareness stage to the CRM alongside budget and timeline, to see whether prospects move along.
2. **Read the keywords** (low-touch, cohorts). He maps the SEMrush search intent types to stages:
   - Informational is roughly stage 2-3.
   - Commercial investigation ("best", "top", "review", "X vs Y", "compare") is stage 3-4.
   - Transactional ("buy", "discount", "coupon", "cheap") is stage 5. A coupon-code search for your SaaS means they are ready to buy.
3. **Use tools that label intent**: SEMrush's dashboard tags keywords I (informational), C (commercial), T (transactional), N (navigational). SimilarWeb has an intent column too (nav, transact, local).

chunks.heading: Stages 1-2: unaware and problem-aware content
chunks.text:
- Stage 1 content is high-level and slow to convert. His example is Session Lab (workshop agendas), with posts like room setup styles and becoming a great facilitator. It likely gets search traffic but takes a long time to turn into customers. This is why he says start at the bottom.
- Stage 2 content solves a specific problem and doesn't mention your product category. Examples from the Micro Conf community:
  - **Ruben (Sewell)**: most of his traffic is organic Google. He gives away contract templates and agreements, drawn from 25,000 sales documents. People need a template and don't yet know they need e-signature software.
  - **Session Lab**: workshop templates.
  - **Veed** (co-founder spoke at Micro Conf Europe): SEO tool pages like add subtitles to video, add music to video, add text to video. Rob's guess is that they pull visitors through with a freemium offering.
  - **UserList** (Benedict and Jane): "What is user onboarding? The Ultimate Guide for SaaS companies".
- Stage 2 content is general (contracts, blog posts) and says nothing about your product.

chunks.heading: Stage 3: solution-aware content and channels
chunks.text:
- Searchers use category terms ("best email marketing software"). Sources include Google, Capterra, G2, Reddit and Quora.
- To check which review site dominates your category, search "best [category]" and "top [category]" in an incognito browser and see whether Capterra, G2 or Software Advice ranks higher. He hopes it's Capterra, "the easiest one to work with and advertise on".
- Capterra ads: people there are usually at stage 3 or 4, so even high cost per click can convert well if you test. Rob points to an interview with a founder "crushing it" with Capterra, found by searching YouTube for "Capterra SaaS marketing" plus his name.
- Monitoring mentions: Rob uses **F5Bot** and **Syften** for Reddit, Hacker News, Twitter, Lobsters, Stack Overflow, Indie Hackers and more.
  - They email or Slack him a few times a week when someone mentions his book, Micro Conf or Tiny Seed.
  - Google Alerts is "useless these days" for him.
  - Anyone naming your product is product-aware by definition (stage 4), so you can join the conversation.
- Content examples: UserList's "SaaS email marketing strategy, everything you need to know" (deeper than their onboarding content).
- Sewell's e-signature funnel walks people through three screens:
  1. What is an electronic signature?
  2. Create your own, with the signature drawn on screen. Rob calls this "engineering as marketing".
  3. "Easy and free e-signatures for all of your documents".
- Rob notes this carries people from stage 2 to stage 4.

chunks.heading: Stage 4: product-aware content (versus, alternative-to, case studies)
chunks.text:
- **Alternative-to pages** target people searching for a competitor (e.g. "alternative to HubSpot, Klaviyo, ActiveCampaign, MailChimp"). Use them in your early days to piggyback on the competitor's brand and SEO.
- **Versus pages** ("your product vs competitor") only work once you have a brand people search for. In your first month or year, almost nobody compares you to a competitor. Rob says to keep these for stage 5.
- UserList has a lot of alternative-to pages because not enough people search versus terms for them yet.
- Rob's incognito test on MailChimp vs Klaviyo: MailChimp ranked 2nd and Klaviyo 3rd, each with passive-aggressive copy. Zapier ranked first, even though it is far up the funnel. Companies like Zapier, HubSpot and Honeybadger go after huge traffic terms and don't mind.
- Case studies belong here. They help close one-on-one outbound sales too.

chunks.heading: Stage 5: most-aware content (features, demos, trust)
chunks.text:
- At this point you "break the paradigm" of benefits-not-features. When someone first finds you, lead with benefits. Deeper in the funnel they need features.
- Examples: Drip's feature pages (built after Rob left), UserList's feature pages, and UserList's knowledge base with a list of integrations. A buyer judges whether the documentation is good.
- **Long-form demos**: go from the 60-second homepage demo to a 30-45 minute demo. Rob says: "If I'm ready to buy software I will 100% watch a 30 minute or 45 minute demo of someone going through it at 2x." It can be pre-recorded.
- Also: versus pages, case studies, white papers (which Rob personally dislikes).
- **Security and compliance content**: Ruben at Sewell published a page on SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, network security and system reliability. A buyer about to purchase cares, while a stage 1-2 reader doesn't.
- HubSpot is his model of a company doing this at every stage (versus pages such as Sales Cloud vs HubSpot Sales, and case studies).

chunks.heading: The 2012-13 Velvet Mail (later Drip) mistake
chunks.text:
- Rob and Derek Reichert started the codebase that became Drip, originally named Velvet Mail. Rob paid a writer roughly $5,000-6,000 for a batch of content before launch, to "start marketing the day you start coding".
- Content was released over about six months and brought "crickets".
- Why it failed: no plan, strategy or framework for prioritizing. Titles were generic and top of funnel: "Seven email marketing myths", "A beginner's guide to email marketing", "Five things to know about email marketing".
- The fix is to prioritize by awareness stage, starting with the lower stages where people are closer to buying.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling surveyed 200+ SaaS founders earning $1k+/month to see how they found their ideas. 72% found them through work: day job problems, copying incumbents, freelancing, or building another product. Each method comes with why it works, pitfalls and self-check questions.

chunks.heading: Rob's survey of 200+ SaaS founders: how they found their ideas
chunks.text:
- Rob surveyed over 200 SaaS founders making at least $1,000/month. Some made well over $100,000/month.
- He wanted data on how founders actually found winning ideas, not opinions or hypothetical idea lists.
- He sees these methods across his own companies, hundreds of startups he's invested in, and thousands of SaaS companies in the TinySeed, MicroConf and Startups For The Rest Of Us ecosystem.
- His long-running line: "Don't tell me your idea, tell me what problem it solves."
- Share of respondents by method:
  - Problem at a day job: 48%
  - Copying or entering an existing product category: about 10%
  - Freelancing or agency work: about 10%
  - Spouse, friend or colleague's problem: 8%
  - Scratching your own itch: 16%
  - Building on an existing product: 4%
  - Finding a problem online: 3%
  - Emerging technology: 3%
- 72% found their idea through work. That covers day-job frustrations, expensive tools they knew they could build better or cheaper, patterns from agency clients, and opportunities found while building something else.
- His conclusion is that "your SaaS idea might be right under your nose."
- His free "9-to-5 audit" at robwalling.com/ideas walks through exercises for spotting opportunities in your workday.
- He is turning the research into a book on finding, choosing and validating an idea, finding product-market fit, and launching a profitable SaaS business.

chunks.heading: Method 1: Find a problem at your day job (48%)
chunks.text:
- This is the most common route. You spot a problem as a frustrated developer or as a subject matter expert who knows the industry's pain points.
- Examples he cites:
  - **Jitbit** (help desk). The founder saw that modern tools lacked "boring" features like SSO, Active Directory integration, user provisioning and on-prem Windows hosting. The tools that had them looked like the '90s. Rob notes the saturated market was a good sign, because "the market was there".
  - **Upstream Edge** (oil and gas well valuation). A petroleum engineer of ten years built a desktop app that is 100 times faster than alternatives.
  - **Didomite** (looping video for public screens). The founder spent years in digital signage and saw the same UX problems repeatedly. He jumped 10 years later.
  - **Blue Gamma** (interest rate forecasts). Two consultants had manually pulled and formatted rate data for clients, sometimes several times a day.
  - **Loody** (formerly Metro Retro). Born from a hackathon prototype after the founder watched a PM hand-write retro notes.
- Why it works:
  - You have deep context on the problem and its workarounds.
  - You have built-in access to customers and beta testers.
  - You understand the buying process: who signs off, budget cycles, objections.
  - You may be able to validate while still employed.
- Watch-outs:
  - Make sure the problem exists beyond your company. Your employer may be uniquely dysfunctional.
  - Check your employment agreement for IP clauses.
  - Don't use proprietary information or customer data.
  - Rob wouldn't use an employer's laptop. He'd work on a personal one and be "really clean about it".
- Questions he suggests asking:
  - Which tools frustrate me or my coworkers daily?
  - Which manual processes should be automated?
  - Are the incumbents actually old and clunky, or just disliked by me?
- Tip: consider old jobs too. Didomite's problem was a decade old.

chunks.heading: Method 2: Enter an existing category (about 10%)
chunks.text:
- Rob says "copy" really means entering an existing category with other players. It does not mean cloning.
- Examples:
  - **t.ly**. The founder's employer was quoted thousands of dollars for a Bitly custom domain. He built an in-house URL shortener over a weekend, then realized others would want a cheaper option.
  - **BigMailer**. The founders had 300,000+ subscribers and found email tools too expensive. They built in-house on Amazon, then productized it.
  - **Checkout Joy**. Local payment processors for LMS platforms in a market without Stripe. The first customers were live within a week, with an immediate conversion bump.
  - **Hururu.ai**. An AI phone answering service for Australian businesses with local accents, modeled on US products like Rosie AI. The founder bet US players wouldn't localize soon.
- Rob's own Drip example (acquired in 2016, a "life-changing exit"):
  - Drip began as an email capture widget plus email sequences.
  - He saw market pull for automation features that cheaper email providers lacked. Existing tools with those features were expensive, used annual contracts, had poor software and required talking to a salesperson.
  - Drip didn't copy a product, but it entered an existing category. Visitors to the homepage immediately understood what it was.
  - He only had to say why Drip was better or different, not explain a novel concept. Positioning moved from email service provider to email automation to lightweight marketing automation.
- Why it works:
  - Demand is already proven.
  - You can read incumbents' negative reviews and support forums.
  - You can differentiate on price, UX, features or niche.
  - Long-standing incumbents often raise prices and go upmarket, which leaves room.
  - In a big market, a small slice can be a great bootstrapped business.
- Watch-outs:
  - Copying in a small market means fighting for scraps. It works best in big markets.
  - "We're newer" is not a differentiator.
  - Incumbents have a head start on brand, SEO, integrations, trust and marketing.
  - "I'll just execute better is not a strategy."
- Questions to ask:
  - Why are customers unhappy: price, features, support or usability?
  - Does my differentiation matter to customers, or only to me?
  - Is there a channel the incumbent uses poorly?
  - Is there an underserved segment?

chunks.heading: Method 3: Freelancing and agency work (about 10%)
chunks.text:
- Examples:
  - **Drum** (ERP for small consulting firms). The founder kept rebuilding similar functionality for clients.
  - **Civic Review** (permitting software). The founder was asked three times by municipalities and built it on the third request.
  - **StatusGator**. Built to solve the founder's own bug-hunting problem: a status page he didn't know about held the cause of a bug. It aggregates status pages and emails on changes.
  - **Dump Truck Dispatcher**. The founder ran a dev shop and kept the IP in return for charging the client less.
- Why it works:
  - You see the same problem across several clients.
  - Clients pay you to learn their problems, which is paid market research.
  - You build domain expertise.
  - Agency revenue can fund early product development.
- Watch-outs:
  - Agency work is demanding, so finding build time is hard.
  - Make sure client contracts make IP ownership clear before productizing. Many consulting and employment agreements sign away what you build, even on your own computer at home.
  - Moving from custom work to product thinking is harder than it looks. You have to learn to say no to feature requests.
  - Don't build something so tailored to one client that nobody else wants it.
- Questions to ask:
  - What functionality have I built three or more times for different clients?
  - What internal agency tools might others want?
  - Do I have a clear path from agency revenue to product revenue, or will I do both forever?
  - Do I want to serve my clients' industry long-term?

chunks.heading: Methods 4 and 5: Problems from people you know, and problems found online
chunks.text:
**Method 4: spouse, friend or colleague (8%)**
- Go hunt for problems by asking your network about their jobs.
- Examples:
  - **Quill Therapy Solutions**. The founder's therapist wife suggested using his AI tool to generate progress notes.
  - **CrankWheel**. A co-founder with years in sales told him that people on a call with a prospect used nothing to show something, because screen-sharing tools were too complex.
- Why it works:
  - You have a direct line to someone with the problem.
  - You can learn without cold calling at first.
  - The relationship creates accountability.
  - They can introduce you to others in the field.
- Watch-outs:
  - Their problem may be unique.
  - They may be too nice to say your solution is weak.
  - Mixing business and personal relationships is complicated.
  - Their expertise plus your building skills isn't enough without understanding the market.
- Questions to ask:
  - What does my spouse or friend complain about at work?
  - Can they give me about five intros?
  - Am I building a business, or doing a favor?
  - Do I have the patience to learn an unfamiliar industry?

**Method 5: finding a problem online (3%)**
- Rob notes this method is often touted online but is hard. Only 3% used it.
- Examples:
  - **String Thing** (Shopify delivery-date app). The founder combed Shopify support forums for complaints. He then checked the app store for apps with many reviews and many negative reviews, which pointed to widespread but poorly solved problems.
  - **Hovercode** (dynamic QR codes). The founder had an interest, talked to a marketing friend, and used Ahrefs to find huge search volume.
- Why it works:
  - You can find problems in industries you've never worked in.
  - You can validate with search volume, complaint counts or community size.
  - Negative reviews of existing products are "a goldmine for differentiation".
- Watch-outs:
  - People complain about things they wouldn't pay for, so signal-to-noise is low.
  - You lack insider context.
  - It takes lots of time and patience.
  - Selling to strangers in an unfamiliar industry is hard.
- Sources he lists:
  - Reddit
  - Facebook groups
  - Private Slack groups
  - Support forums
  - G2, Capterra and app store reviews
  - Ahrefs, Semrush and Google Keyword Planner
  - 75+ marketplaces at microconf.com/marketplaces, if you want to build an add-on for an existing platform
- Questions to ask:
  - Is the complaint repeated by many people?
  - Would they pay, or just vent?
  - Can I reach them?
  - Will I invest the time to learn the industry?
- A real-world variant is **OrderNerd**. A co-founder saw a wall of delivery tablets (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub) in a restaurant and heard the staff's pain. The founders had five years of restaurant sales and a decade of third-party API experience. Rob's lesson is to stay curious and observant.

chunks.heading: Method 6: Scratch your own itch (16%), and how Rob validates it
chunks.text:
- Basecamp (DHH and Jason Fried) popularized this in the early and mid-2000s. Rob says it's "certainly not a bad way", but many things have to line up.
- "You can't just say, 'I have a problem, therefore that's validation.'" That only validates one customer paying $0, yourself.
- Rob's own validation of Drip, which began as an itch he had:
  - He asked 17 other founders he knew whether they had the problem.
  - He got 10 or 11 yeses before building.
- Examples:
  - **Dialog Shift** (AI for hotels). The founders were frustrated as hotel guests by how hard it was to get simple information, such as breakfast times or yoga class schedules.
  - **Simple Booklet**. The founder had sold an earlier business and sailed for 11 years. He found paper brochures hard to use, and noticed that every print brochure started as a PDF.
- Why it works:
  - You understand the problem intimately.
  - You're motivated.
  - You are your own first user.
  - Your passion shows in marketing and sales.
- Watch-outs:
  - You may be a market of one.
  - You may build what you want rather than what the market wants.
  - Your use case may be too niche.
  - Founders underestimate how different their needs are from typical customers.
- Questions to ask:
  - How many others have this exact problem, and can I talk to them?
  - Am I a representative user or an edge case?
  - Would I pay more to solve it, or is it mildly annoying?
  - Can I separate my preferences from market needs?

chunks.heading: Methods 7 and 8: Emerging technology (3%) and building on an existing product (4%)
chunks.text:
**Method 7: emerging or fast-growing technology**
- Rob calls this "every developer's dream", but rarely do people turn it into a business. Only 3% did.
- Examples include AI, a new API, or a new platform opening up (Facebook, Shopify, Squarespace, HubSpot).
- Cases:
  - **WA Notifier**. A former WordPress agency owner bet that WhatsApp marketing would follow email marketing, especially in India, GCC countries and South America. The timing coincided with WhatsApp opening to new API partners.
  - **Gen Text AI**. Word add-ins built right after ChatGPT launched, by a consultant and economist who used Office heavily.
  - **PodSqueeze**. Rob's podcast uses it. It generates posts, clips, summaries and transcripts from audio or video. The founder built it from his own post-production frustration right after ChatGPT launched.
- Why it works:
  - Early movers establish themselves before the market crowds.
  - New technology creates new problems.
  - You ride the attention.
  - Customers forgive rough edges.
- Watch-outs:
  - Too early means the technology or customers aren't ready. Too late means dozens or hundreds of competitors.
  - The hype cycle can mislead you.
  - The technology may not mature as expected.
  - Well-funded players move fast.
- Questions to ask:
  - Is the technology ready for real use, or still experimental?
  - Are businesses already spending in adjacent areas?
  - Do I have a unique angle, or am I chasing hype?
  - Can I build something useful before the window closes?

**Method 8: building on an existing product**
- You're working on one product and find a bigger or better opportunity. Rob says these were new products, not necessarily pivots.
- Examples:
  - **Authored Up**. The founders built a hiring product without talking to customers (no Mom Test). They then made an internal LinkedIn content tool for their own outreach.
  - **Super Data**. A YouTube transcript scraper for another product became an API. The founder monetized it on RapidAPI and it "snowballed".
  - **SignWell**. Founders saw customers' dissatisfaction with e-signature tools while running another business.
- Why it works:
  - You're already in the market, talking to customers.
  - You have momentum, skills and sometimes revenue.
  - An internal tool may have broader demand.
  - You reuse what you've learned.
- Watch-outs:
  - Shiny objects. The new idea must be better, not just more exciting.
  - Splitting focus between two products can kill both.
  - You may be running from hard problems in your current product.
  - Sunk cost can cloud your judgment.
- Questions to ask:
  - Is this genuinely bigger and better, or am I bored?
  - Can I validate quickly without abandoning the current product?
  - Do I have resources for both?
  - What would have to be true for the switch to be worth it?
- Rob says validation comes next once you've found an idea, and he covers it in a follow-up video.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling argues that early SaaS founders should start marketing before coding, and build a network rather than a social audience. He lays out six repeatable tactics for finding the first 10 customers: talk to founders, tap your network, find existing audiences, lurk in communities, do outreach, and run ads for learning.

chunks.heading: Market first: market before you code, and don't confuse it with building an audience
chunks.text:
- Rob argues founders should start marketing before they start coding. He says this is repeatable and predictable, so you learn from it. Luck teaches nothing: "It's like buying a lottery ticket and winning."
- He separates marketing from "building in public". Marketing means talking to prospective customers, not to other indie hackers or founders on social media.
- Of his 191 investments in B2B SaaS companies, fewer than 5% had any kind of audience. That count includes social media, podcast and YouTube audiences.
- His advice: "Build your network, not your audience." Learning marketing as a skill matters far more than building an audience.
- He calls treating X (Twitter) as a marketing strategy, or building a following to become a SaaS founder, a big beginner mistake. A handful of people succeed that way and tens of thousands try. He compares it to saying "I want to play in the NBA" or "I want to be Taylor Swift."
- Marketing includes content people want to consume, SEO, pay-per-click ads, integrations and partnerships, direct outreach, in-person events and podcast appearances.
- He has listed 20 marketing approaches for B2B SaaS in his book "The SaaS Playbook".
- Learning to market repeatably carries over to every product you start afterward.

chunks.heading: Setting up before the first conversations: landing page, early-access list and ICP
chunks.text:
- Rob starts with a basic landing page and an early-access list.
- How hands-on he is depends on whether the product will use high-touch sales and demos or a self-serve approach.
- He picks an ideal customer profile (ICP), maybe two. If you think your product suits everyone online, "good luck." He says you are in for a really hard time.
- Self-funded founders especially need a tight ICP, which ties to going niche.
- An ICP can be an industry (construction company owners, gym owners, martial arts schools). It can also be a job title in a company (HR manager, software development manager, engineer).
- The test is who is most likely to need, want and buy the product.
- A list of interested people is an asset. You can survey it, for example:
  - Ask what they want the product to include.
  - Send a screenshot of what you're building, or a value proposition you're considering, and ask what they think.
- You can also poll visitors on the landing page. Collect anonymous feedback first, then ask for their email address after they give it.
- He calls embedding short surveys in the flow a somewhat advanced approach, but one he sees successful founders use.

chunks.heading: Four ways to start conversations with potential customers (founders, network, audiences, communities)
chunks.text:
- **Talk to other founders** who sold into the same space or to the same ICP. Talk to those who succeeded and those who failed.
- **Talk to sales and marketing people at somewhat bigger companies.** He means not huge ones. His example is a software company making $50K a month in the same space or selling to the same customers. Find someone on LinkedIn and say something like "Hey, I'm trying to do this thing and I need some advice."
- **Use your existing network.** Reach out to people you know in the industry for insights and ask them to introduce you to people who might want the product. If you know no one in the industry, he says you've made a mistake. You should build your network in the space you plan to sell in.
- **Find an audience online that you can reach.** He stresses finding one, not building your own, because building takes years. Examples are:
  - Podcast appearances.
  - Someone in your network willing to tweet about you or share your ideas with their audience.
- **Lurk in online communities.** Join Facebook groups, subreddits, Slack channels and other relevant forums. Watch for common problems and complaints people have with existing solutions in your space.

chunks.heading: Direct outreach (warm or cold) as a core early tactic
chunks.text:
- Rob counts direct outreach as the fifth tactic. It can be warm or cold, by email, LinkedIn or Twitter DMs.
- He says few aspiring founders do it. They assume everything is about inbound traffic, which can work. He leans toward outreach himself because he is a developer turned marketer.
- His example is Tally (tally.so). Co-founder Marie appeared on his podcast in episode 717. She cold-contacted thousands of people to get started.
- He pushes back on copying success blindly, such as "they had a free plan, so I'll have a free plan." In his view what made Tally succeed was:
  - A free plan in a very broad market at low cost to serve.
  - Hard work.
  - Things like cold outreach that probably felt uncomfortable.
- His point is that it will make you uncomfortable too, and that is fine.

chunks.heading: Using early feedback to shape the product
chunks.text:
- Rob warns against launching a landing page with a fixed picture of what you'll build. Founders are makers, so they just build.
- Feedback arrives in conversations on Reddit, Zoom or email. Some of it reinforces your vision and some says you're heading the wrong way. Typical asks are "Can you add this?", "Can you pivot to this?" and "Can you support my use case?"
- He calls learning to take feedback from prospects and others a skill you must develop to last as an entrepreneur. This means learning who to listen to and how to adapt your product vision and marketing copy to what the market demands.
- Without that, the odds of succeeding with your first idea are very low.
- The goal of the first 10 customers is sales, a launch list and learning (what to build, how to adjust course, how to improve it). He says it is all of these.
- A common first-time-founder mistake is not knowing which feedback to heed and how to adjust your messaging and vision.
- Decide whether you want to find a unique niche or compete in an established market. If you pick a unique niche, validate with customers early that anyone cares.
- If you can't find your people online, you may need traditional marketing, which is hard. It takes lots of cold outreach and in-person events. Or you start over in a space where people look for solutions online.
- Even with a low-touch path, you must talk to people to learn what you're building and where the market will lead you.

chunks.heading: Sixth tactic: run ads to find early adopters
chunks.text:
- Rob's sixth tactic is running Facebook, LinkedIn and Google ads to start those early conversations and find true early adopters for your first 10 customers.
- The goal is not positive ROI. It is to get people into the funnel and find interested prospects who might fit your product.
- It doesn't work for everyone. You need a budget and have to learn to run ads. He says many free resources and inexpensive video courses teach it.
- Finding the first 10 is not the end. You then need a marketing strategy that brings in new customers on a regular basis.
- He promotes his SaaS Launchpad video course (SaaSLaunchpad.co): 27 modules and about 10 hours of video, built on lessons from thousands of startups he has watched and worked with over 20 years.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling covers the five marketing approaches he sees working repeatedly for B2B SaaS (alternative-search SEO, PPC, signal-based cold outreach, integration marketing, content marketing) and how AI changes each. He closes with a three-factor framework (speed, cost, scalability) for picking one fast and one slow channel.

chunks.heading: The "big five" B2B SaaS marketing strategies and how Rob picks among them
chunks.text:
Rob has invested in more than 230 SaaS companies. He says five B2B SaaS marketing strategies work "over and over and over again":
- SEO (search beyond Google)
- Pay-per-click advertising
- Cold outreach
- Integration marketing (plus partnerships)
- Content marketing

AI changes how each one works, but it does not remove the fundamentals. The full SaaS Playbook lists 20 B2B SaaS marketing approaches. The other 15 are used less often or depend on market and annual contract value (ACV). The playbook is the basis for the video.

chunks.heading: SEO: rank in the search engines where your customer actually searches
chunks.text:
- Rob says Google is one of many search engines. YouTube is number two. Amazon is number three or four, depending on the source.
- Other search engines where an ideal customer may be searching, often with easier ranking than Google:
  - iOS App Store
  - WordPress plugin repository
  - Reddit
  - Wikipedia
  - Shopify App Store
  - Adobe App Store
  - Chrome Web Store
- Examples:
  - At Drip, his last startup, the team deliberately built two WordPress plugins and ranked them for email marketing terms in the WordPress plugin repository.
  - Tiny Seed founders build Chrome plugins to rank in the Chrome Web Store for terms that fit their ICP. The plugin extends the app's functionality and is not a random side project.
  - He has seen founders write Kindle or physical books to rank in Amazon search.
- Key insight: find where your ideal customer is searching. Many of those places are easier to rank in than Google.
- Impact of AI:
  - Anyone can now build a WordPress plugin with Claude Code in a few hours, which could crowd the repo.
  - AEO (answer engine optimization, also called AI SEO or GEO) is now a thing. LLMs like ChatGPT and Perplexity pull content to answer queries directly.
  - The Google SEO principles still work for AEO. Quality content that directly answers questions still wins. Structured content and clear answers matter more than ever.
  - Google still processes hundreds of times more queries than ChatGPT. He says traditional SEO "is not dead and will not be anytime soon."

chunks.heading: Pay-per-click ads: price point and payback period decide whether they work
chunks.text:
- PPC is the fastest way to get traffic. It is also the fastest way to burn budget if you don't know what you're doing.
- Major platforms:
  - Google
  - Facebook
  - Instagram
  - YouTube
  - Amazon
  - Capterra
  - LinkedIn
  - Marketplaces with their own ads, such as the Shopify App Store
- Ads work when you:
  - need speed
  - have budget to test and refine
  - can measure customer acquisition cost (CAC) against lifetime value (LTV)
  - charge enough per month for a reasonable payback period
- Payback rule for bootstrappers:
  - They usually need a 3-6 month payback period.
  - A one-year payback only works with a lot of money in the bank or venture backing.
  - At $20 a month, that implies a maximum of $60-$120 to acquire a customer. He says you are unlikely to find an ad network that cheap today.
- Price rule of thumb:
  - He would not consider ads below roughly $40-$50 a month unless he could find extremely cheap clicks of 10, 20 or 30 cents that also convert at a workable rate.
  - He is not saying $10-$20 a month can't work, but he hasn't seen costs in a long time that allow break-even at those prices.
  - B2C plays at $4, $10 or $15 a month are limited by low average revenue per account and generally can't run ads.
- Upside: if ads work, they are "like a spigot you can just turn on and off." He grew more than one SaaS company almost purely on ads and added tens of thousands of dollars of MRR. He did it by investing money and time, carefully testing and tweaking creative, copy and targeting. He says ads are difficult with SaaS but not impossible.
- Impact of AI:
  - AI generates ad copy and more creatives to split test faster and cheaper.
  - Everyone has the same tools, so competition gets noisier.
  - Targeting, the offer, the landing page and human oversight matter more than clever AI copy. "AI won't save you from a lack of strategy."
  - New AI-native ad platforms are emerging. ChatGPT ads are coming, and maybe Perplexity. He expects products that keep prices low or offer free tools to monetize through them.

chunks.heading: Cold outreach: the signal is timing plus fit
chunks.text:
- Rob says most cold outreach deserves its bad reputation, but when it works, "it really works."
- What separates outreach that converts from outreach that is ignored is the signal. The signal is the prospect's timing plus the fit of your tool. You need businesses that need what you built and a sign that they need it now.
- Drip example:
  - Infusionsoft (now Keap) was a big competitor, and its customers signed one-year contracts.
  - Drip kept an ongoing list of new Infusionsoft customers and contacted them about eight months into the contract, when renewal was coming up.
  - The message asked whether they wanted to explore other options. In many cases they did.
- Key insight: "cold outreach without a signal is spam and cold outreach with a signal is helpful."
- Impact of AI:
  - AI handles personalization at scale: custom intros, prospect analysis and automatic sequences.
  - Everyone has the same tools, so the signal matters more than ever. "AI can personalize, but it can't create timing."
  - Gmail and Microsoft now reject non-compliant bulk email, so deliverability infrastructure matters more.

chunks.heading: Integration marketing and partnerships: build only when both sides promote
chunks.text:
- Rob says many founders sleep on this. It improves the product and brings in customers, and when it works it produces leads for years.
- How to find opportunities: ask what steps happen before and after someone uses your product.
  - Example for a podcast show-notes app: before it, recording, editing and inviting guests; after it, posting to WordPress or uploading to YouTube or Spotify.
  - Unless you will build those features yourself, find tools already doing the before and after steps. Ask them to integrate and to promote the integration.
- Rule: "Don't build the integration unless both sides agree to promote it."
- The seven promotion options he offered partners at his last startup:
  1. Blog post
  2. Email to both partners' lists
  3. Tweet or social post
  4. Knowledge base article
  5. In-app mention
  6. Webinar
  7. Listing in an add-on marketplace
- His pitch was to do all seven as long as the partner does all seven, and otherwise to match whichever ones they do.
- Results and process at his last SaaS:
  - The team built roughly 30-35 integrations in about 18 months. Integration marketing was a key growth driver.
  - Start with an MVP "1.0" integration, such as customers pasting in an API key instead of a full OAuth build.
  - Launch, co-promote and see whether it drives leads and usage.
  - With a couple thousand customers, some integrations had only a handful of users. Those were not built out further.
  - Track which integrations are popular and drive new customers, then build V2.0 and V3.0 versions. Add OAuth, make setup easier and support more actions.
- Partnerships are the same idea with no code written. It is reciprocal promotion to each other's audiences using one or more of the seven options, recommending each other's tool.
- Partner assets (articles, forum posts, knowledge base articles) keep converting long after launch.
- Impact of AI:
  - Integrations are technically easier to build, with faster development and better documentation.
  - MCP (Model Context Protocol) is emerging as a standard for connecting AI agents to APIs. Vendors increasingly ship MCP endpoints, much as REST APIs spread in the 2010s. He says MCP-native is expected to be core product functionality for many launches by the end of 2026.
  - The marketing side (partnerships, co-promotion, relationships) "is still a human game" that the founder must do.

chunks.heading: Content marketing: virality versus audience building
chunks.text:
- Content is not only blog posts. It can be a book, a podcast, a YouTube channel or a free course. The key question is whether you are building for virality or for an audience over time, which he calls "two very different games."
- Content often pairs with SEO but can also work purely on people sharing it.
- Virality: aim for the top of Hacker News, Reddit or other social news sites to drive visitors who convert to trials.
- Audience building: slow, steady growth over time.
- Warning:
  - Building a media brand alongside a SaaS product is only for very well-funded companies or people exceptionally gifted at it.
  - He thinks only about 10%, at most 20%, of SaaS founders should do founder-led marketing with video, audio or YouTube.
- Execution: most founders produce content themselves because they lack money. Hire production help later as revenue grows.
- Impact of AI:
  - AI helps produce content faster: outlines, drafts and repurposing, such as turning a video into an essay or blog post.
  - The bar for standing out is rising sharply because of the "AI slop tsunami."
  - Original thinking, proprietary data and real expertise become more valuable. The human touch wins through original research, customer voices, and first-hand experience and opinions.
- Rob mentions a MicroConf talk on the five stages of customer awareness and how to match content to each stage.

chunks.heading: The three-factor framework: speed, cost and scalability
chunks.text:
Rob uses this to choose which marketing approach to focus on. Price point changes everything.

1. **Speed:** how long until results arrive (weeks, months or years) and how long you can afford to wait. Early on, favor fast approaches, though they may not scale. As the company matures, add slower approaches.
2. **Cost:** hard dollars plus your time.
   - Early on, think in dollars rather than your time.
   - Higher ACV means more money to invest in marketing, and more approaches open up as you raise prices.
   - With a very low price point, only about four or five of the 20 playbook approaches are available.
   - At $30,000 a year, all 20 are available.
3. **Scalability:** whether you can reach more people by turning the dial.
   - Low scalability: one-time events like Product Hunt launches or Quora posts.
   - High scalability: SEO and pay-per-click ads.

Practical advice:
- Work one fast approach and one slow approach at the same time.
  - Fast only means you are always chasing leads.
  - Slow only means you starve while waiting for traction.
- A common pairing is cold outreach (fast) plus SEO (slow).
- You don't need dozens of approaches. SaaS companies growing to seven or eight figures can often do it on one or two channels that scale well.
- Find what's working and double down. Adding two or three new approaches scatters you too much.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2021 MicroConf Europe talk on practical SaaS pricing. Rob argues for building expansion revenue via value metrics or feature gating, prioritizing average revenue per customer over LTV, and raising prices because higher-paying customers churn less and unlock more marketing channels. He also gives a framework for experiment vs certainty, grandfathering, and messaging.

chunks.heading: Expansion revenue as the SaaS pricing "cheat code"
chunks.text:
- Rob says recurring revenue is the business cheat code: it lifts sales multiple, enterprise value and stability, including in a recession. SaaS founders get it for free.
- Expansion revenue is "the opportunity for a customer to pay you more money as they get more value from your product." It usually works through pricing tiers that auto-upgrade customers.
- First-order effect: more revenue per customer. Second-order effect: it can get you to net negative churn.
- Net negative churn example: a month with zero net new customers where the business still grew 4.5%.
- Rob says the biggest, fastest-growing SaaS businesses reach net negative churn. It is not possible for every SaaS, but worth striving for.
- If he started another SaaS, he would build in some virality and some expansion revenue. He would also never again build a product that sends email.
- The goal is to charge more, but only to the right customer segments.
- SquadCast example (a Tiny Seed batch 2 company, studio-quality podcast recording):
  - Hobbyist podcasts (fly fishing, Dungeons & Dragons) balk at $9-14 a month.
  - Business podcasts like Startups for the Rest of Us would find $50-100 a month trivial.
  - Big networks (Gimlet, NPR, ESPN, iHeartRadio) should pay thousands a month, roughly $2-5K.
  - Ask which features or usage patterns separate these segments, so customers land in the right bucket at signup or upgrade over time.
- This covers monthly or annual pricing only. In the State of Independent SaaS report, about 85-90% of respondents are monthly or annual, about 3% pay-as-you-go and about 4% metered.

chunks.heading: Value metrics, feature gating and when to combine them
chunks.text:
- Rob ranks three ways to build upgrade paths into monthly pricing:
  1. **Value metric** (his number one): the more you use, the more value you get. Examples: contacts or subscribers for Mailchimp and Drip, seats for Close, Salesforce and Pipedrive.
  2. **Feature gating**: use it when no usage number fits. Examples: a Salesforce or Zapier integration, or direct streaming to YouTube, on a higher plan.
  3. **Both together**: more common in larger companies.
- Seat-based pricing rule: only use it if two users in the same company see different things when they log in.
  - Pipedrive (assigned deals) and Help Scout (assigned tickets) pass this test.
  - Mailchimp-style tools fail it, because users can share one login.
- Castos (podcast hosting) uses feature gating without a value metric.
  - Early hosts offered unlimited podcasts and episodes around 2008-2010, which locked the space in.
  - Gated features include video republishing to YouTube, Headliner audiogram integration and advanced analytics.
  - Rob runs two podcasts on the $190 plan and Startups for the Rest of Us on the $490 tier.
- Rails Autoscale (Heroku add-on) does both neatly. The value metric is the number of dynos (1 to 3, 1 to 9, 1 to 29). The feature gate is the dyno type, since performance dynos cost more than standard ones.
- AWeber competes with Mailchimp using "everyone gets everything" pricing, which Rob calls a clever jiu-jitsu move.
- Don't combine both early. Mailchimp (sold for $12 billion), Zapier, Salesforce and Intercom all have complex pages, but none started that way.
  - Mailchimp's 2007 pricing was one plan based purely on subscribers.
  - Rob finds even Mailchimp's current page daunting, and he built an ESP.
  - Under about $1M ARR, he would sacrifice some MRR to stay simple and win customers.

chunks.heading: ARPC beats LTV, and why higher ARPC unlocks marketing channels
chunks.text:
- Rob prefers ARPC (average revenue per customer) to ARPU, since "users are not customers."
- LTV is ARPC divided by churn. $50 a month at 5% churn gives $1,000. At 1% churn it gives $5,000, but that is collected over 8.33 years.
- Low churn can make LTV deceiving. Bootstrappers lack the cash to wait years, so they should focus on ARPC.
- CAC payback rules of thumb:
  - Venture-backed: spend up to about 12 months of ACV on acquisition.
  - Bootstrapped: three to six months of revenue, and he once reached seven when cash in the bank was high.
- The only usual ways to raise ARPC are expansion revenue or higher prices.
- Second-order effect: higher ARPC or ACV unlocks more B2B marketing channels. He drew the channel list from Traction by Gabriel Weinberg, the Tiny Seed playbook and his own notes.
  - About $500 a year per customer: only three or four channels are affordable. That supports a $200-300K business, but not seven figures.
  - About $5,000 ACV: roughly half to 60% of channels.
  - $25-50K ACV (enterprise): almost every channel.
- Raising prices therefore also expands which growth strategies are open to you, beyond extra profit.

chunks.heading: The impact of raising prices: first-order and second-order effects
chunks.text:
- Pricing is "one of the biggest levers we have as SaaS founders." It takes only a changed number on a pricing page and in Stripe. The barrier is emotional: fear of crushing the business. Rob helps founders treat it as an experiment.
- Tiny Seed data (anonymous): after the pricing playbook month, several companies changed prices and saw a major change in their MRR graphs.
  - One company's projection without a price change was just over $10K MRR. By March of the next year it was almost $20K.
  - Rob caveats that those graphs also reflect funding and going full-time.
  - Prices can't rise infinitely. There is a ceiling for your market and product, but most founders never reach it.
- Second-order effect: "lower paying customers churn faster." Rob has said this for over a decade.
- Tiny Seed company data, segment A ($30 a month) versus segment B ($100 and up, 80% of revenue):
  - Segment A had net revenue churn of 11%.
  - Segment B had net revenue churn of -4% (net negative).
  - Rob says that single metric can mean the difference between $250K ARR and $1M ARR or more.
- He recommends segmenting churn by price paid or tier. The higher-paying customers are usually where the long-term value is.
- Gather (visual spec management for interior designers and architects, Tiny Seed batch 1):
  - It started with a one- or two-demo-close sales process and a lowest price of $29 a month, which Rob calls unfeasible.
  - They raised to $39 and $79, saw no change in conversion or churn, then moved to $99 with still no difference.
  - Today they charge $165 and $290 and are at their fastest growth rate ever.
  - Reasoning: for a 5-20 person firm running much of its workflow on the tool, $30 versus $130 is a rounding error.
  - Two effects drove the growth: higher prices, and customers who churn less.

chunks.heading: Tactics for raising ARPC without a headline price hike
chunks.text:
- Reduce what a plan includes. At Drip he moved a plan from 3,000 subscribers to 2,500 at the same $49 price. Rob wanted to keep price points like $49.99 and $149, not awkward ones like $59 or $109.
- Drop the lowest plan. Hide the div, watch for a week, and usually nothing changes.
  - Don't do this if you want early adopters to enter at the bottom and upgrade over time, as Mailchimp does.
- Annual plans: Rob loves them.
  - Two months free is about a 16.7% discount.
  - A customer who pays you for 10 months up front can make acquisition cost effectively negative. With $500 CAC and $1,000 collected, you net $500 immediately.
  - Churn also drops and bootstrappers get cash sooner.
- Killing a free plan:
  - He killed HitTail's free plan, which had about 1,500 free users and had been around for five years.
  - The service was losing money with it. He comped a few exceptions, such as a professor.
  - Killing the free plan reduced server load.
  - Free users rarely convert to a $29 plan, so he generally grandfathers them.
- Wide gaps between tiers, such as free or $50 versus $1,000 or more a month:
  - He likes the idea of a "dual funnel," with many $10 customers and some paying thousands.
  - Case by case, complaints may come mainly from low-paying customers.
- Enterprise annual contracts: build in annual increases of 5% to 10% up front, for example "as we renew it'll go up seven percent." Pushback is rare.
- Add-ons versus tiers: Rob has no framework yet and says so.

chunks.heading: Raising prices: experiment or certainty
chunks.text:
- First decide whether the increase is an experiment or a "certainty" (his quotation marks). He decides by gut feel. If he doesn't know, it's an experiment.
- Experiment:
  - Make it a two-minute rollback. Keep all the changes in one Git label.
  - Watch daily: traffic, trial-to-paid conversion, and conversion versus the prior week.
  - Run it for a couple of weeks to a month. He calls this a "poor man's split test."
  - True split testing is very hard. The only company he knows that did it is Zapier, which forked users after signup inside the app so pricing wasn't visible publicly.
- Certainty: he has raised prices knowing he would not roll back, even if the funnel took a short-term hit.
  - Make it a marketable event, a lesson he took from Dharmesh Shah of HubSpot.
  - Drip, 2015 tweet: "Drip's pricing goes up tomorrow. Existing customers/trials are grandfathered. If you've considered Drip, now is a good time."
  - Email existing customers (grandfathered or not), email trial users that the price will be higher if they return, and promote it to the whole marketing list.
  - Drip got a bunch more trials from this.

chunks.heading: Grandfathering rules, including Rob's Rule of Ten
chunks.text:
- Ideally you would just upgrade everyone, as a restaurant does. SaaS has a contract-like expectation, so you must communicate.
- Reasons to grandfather: churn to competitors, angry customers and support burden, and brand damage from doing it poorly. On pure business terms he would raise for everyone.
- Minimum notice if not grandfathering: at least two months, with three more comfortable.
  - Three to six months works. Netflix gives a year and people are still angry.
  - Six months is long enough that people forget and assume you're raising again.
- **Rob's Rule of Ten:** if raising prices on existing customers won't grow MRR by at least 10%, it is probably not worth considering.
  - Example: at $50K MRR, growing by $5K doesn't justify the support burden, brand risk and churn. Going to $57.5K starts getting interesting, and going to $60K may be worth it.
- Never promise "grandfathered for life." You may want to stop grandfathering the next time you raise prices or sell the company. Lifetime deals belong to one-time sales, not SaaS.
- Zombie customers (inactive for 24 months): Rob would probably email everybody, but says it's the founder's call.
  - He says 15-35% of SaaS customers are zombies, and high-pressure marketing tools may see a third to 40%.
  - His own customers received a monthly invoice anyway.
- Developers tend to say "always grandfather," and salespeople "never." Rob says it is a business decision with nuance.

chunks.heading: How to message a price increase (CartHook example)
chunks.text:
- Rob holds up Jordan Gal's CartHook increase as the model. It raised prices a lot, increased fees and didn't grandfather, yet landed well.
  - He grandfathered for six months, through Black Friday, since CartHook served e-commerce.
  - The post is archived on the Wayback Machine (bit.ly/carthookpricing).
- If you grandfather, you only need about three of the six points (explain the change, tell customers they pay nothing more, thank them). If you don't, cover all six:
  1. Set the stage: we're raising prices, here's who we are and how long we've been around.
  2. Give a high-level justification, for example that the product has evolved from an email service to marketing automation and provides far more value.
  3. Give specifics on who is affected and when (optional).
  4. Give more justification (optional).
  5. Say what the commitment is: you have to earn customers over the next six months so they don't churn. Treat customers as free to leave, not prisoners.
  6. Invite questions and reach out.
- The worst increase Rob saw broke all the rules:
  - It gave two weeks' notice and roughly doubled the price.
  - The email was unclear about the new price and gave no justification or commitment.
- His summary: study people who did it poorly and avoid that, and study those who did it well and copy it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob lays out a systematic way to choose marketing channels for a bootstrapped SaaS: ask where customers hang out and where you have an advantage, score approaches by ICE, then pair one fast channel with one slow, scalable one. He argues social posting isn't marketing and that you should commit months before judging a channel.

chunks.heading: How Rob chooses a first SaaS marketing channel: two questions
chunks.text:
- Rob says there is no one-size-fits-all way to market a SaaS company. His book *The SaaS Playbook* lists 20 B2B SaaS marketing approaches he has seen people use. A free sample chapter is at saasplaybook.com.
- Examples he names from the 20: content, SEO, pay-per-click ads, cold outreach, partnerships and integrations (grouped as one approach), affiliate marketing, free tools, hangouts and Q&A sites.
- To pick where to start, he asks two questions:
  1. **Where do your customers hang out, and where do they look for a solution like yours?**
     - If they go to Google, try SEO.
     - If they go to YouTube, get interviewed on other people's channels, or make videos that answer the questions people ask when trying to solve the problem.
     - If you have the budget, buy pay-per-click ads instead of doing SEO.
     - Cold outreach (email, LinkedIn DMs, X/Twitter) works for finding qualified people.
  2. **Do you have an advantage with any of the approaches?** He does not mean "which do I want to do?", which he calls "a terrible question".

chunks.heading: Do the marketing you don't want to do
chunks.text:
- Rob uses a weight-loss comparison: to get fit you eat spinach and work out, not ice cream. Building a business works the same way.
- If you only want to write code and post to Twitter, he says to "go find a hobby" and not start a SaaS company. Success requires doing things you don't want to do, and marketing and sales may be two of them.
- Posting to Twitter and social media "does not count as marketing". He rejects "I'm building an audience so I can someday sell my SaaS to it".
- He recommends approaches that move the needle: content, SEO, cold outreach, free tools, affiliate marketing, hangouts and Q&A sites.
- He describes the typical failure as a founder who codes for 6 months, launches on Product Hunt or posts once on Reddit, and hears crickets.

chunks.heading: Scoring channels with ICE in a spreadsheet
The three-factor framework: pick one fast and one slow approach
chunks.text:
- Rob applies his three-factor framework to marketing approaches. The factors are:
  - **Speed:** how quickly it works.
  - **Cost:** usually dollars, but it can be time.
  - **Scalability:** how far it scales.
- Nothing is fast, cheap and highly scalable. If you find such an approach, "you are very, very lucky".
- Example: posting on Q&A sites or answering Reddit threads is fast and low cost but not very scalable.
- After the ICE analysis he picks **one fast approach and one slow approach**.
  - Fast approaches can get a customer "tomorrow or today", for example cold and warm outreach, including DMing people he knows.
  - Slow approaches such as content and SEO can take about 6 months. They are usually more scalable and build a flywheel.
- The aim is long-term growth from the slow channel and customers now from the fast one.

chunks.heading: How long to run a channel before quitting
chunks.text:
- Rob learns the approach, executes hard, and grinds until it clearly works or clearly doesn't.
- **It's working if it brings in leads:** people he is having conversations with.
- If leads arrive but nobody signs up or buys, there are two possible causes, and telling them apart is a judgment call:
  - no product-market fit (the product doesn't solve a problem people want);
  - the wrong prospects are coming in.
- Time to invest before pulling the plug:
  - most approaches: at least 2 to 3 months;
  - SEO: 6 or more months.
- Example with cold outreach: early on the message, list, copy and maybe the product won't be great. So he doesn't send emails for a week and conclude it failed. He studies how to do it, executes for months, and tunes if results are mediocre. If he gets no results after several months, he probably pulls the plug.
- Winning channels tend to have "asymmetric upside". He says you don't need 5 or 10 approaches to build a successful product. One or two that work well can grow month after month, though you must keep innovating and pushing on them.

chunks.heading: The "Big Five" channels most bootstrapped founders should start with
chunks.text:
- For founders who don't want to work it out from scratch, Rob says roughly 80% should start with his "Big Five", listed in no particular order:
  1. Content
  2. SEO
  3. Pay-per-click ads
  4. Cold outreach
  5. Partnerships and integrations
- He chose them because they are by far the five most-used B2B SaaS approaches among bootstrapped and mostly bootstrapped founders.
- His evidence is his 212 B2B SaaS investments, the tens of thousands of SaaS founders he interacts with through his books, podcast and accelerator, and what he sees working in TinySeed.
- He says he suspects content marketing will be the choice for many founders.
- He claims a content framework that has helped portfolio companies reach their first $100,000 in ARR. He says he shares it with every founder he invests in, but the details aren't given in this source.
- His book *Start Marketing the Day You Start Coding* (2011, revised about 2 years before this video) is the basis for much of the framework.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob argues every SaaS needs four skills covered by the founding team: product, development, marketing and sales. Missing one caps the whole business. He lays out four failure archetypes (builder, marketer, outsourcer, vibe coder), three paths to fill gaps, and revenue-based timelines for delegating each skill.

chunks.heading: The "core four" SaaS skills and why missing one caps the business
chunks.text:
- Rob says that after working with thousands of founders and investing in more than 230 SaaS companies, a stuck SaaS is usually missing one of four skills. His examples of "stuck" are $5-10K MRR, or not reaching $1K MRR.
- The four skills, in no particular order, are product, development, marketing and sales.
- Founders usually think they can fix a gap with an agency, a freelancer or a co-founder. Rob says "almost every time, this doesn't work".
- Rob treats company success as a multiplier: founder × product × market, each scored 1-10. The factors multiply, they don't add.
  - A founder scored 3 (missing sales and marketing) with a 9 market and an 8 product gives 216.
  - A founder scored 7 across all four skills, with the same product and market, gives 504. That is nearly 2.5x the outcome.
  - He calls the numbers directional, not exact.
- His example of close to 10 × 10 × 10 is Jason Cohen's WP Engine: a 9-10 founder, a growing market and a smart product idea.

chunks.heading: What each core skill means: product, development, sales
chunks.text:
- **Product:**
  - It is knowing what to build, in what order, why and how. That includes how a feature integrates into the existing application.
  - It is not project management. It means taking customer feedback and understanding the space and niche. The aim is something people will pay for month after month.
  - Rob says "You can't build something people want by accident." He calls it the founder's job and says most people underestimate how hard it is.
- **Development:**
  - It is more than writing code. It means shipping fast and keeping a codebase that doesn't collapse, so technical debt doesn't hurt 12 months later.
  - Feature velocity is one of a small company's only real advantages over bigger entrenched competitors. With no bureaucracy, a small team can ship in days what takes big companies months.
- **Sales:**
  - It covers real conversations with prospects, handling objections, closing deals and dealing with procurement.
  - Purely self-serve products can skip it. But the fastest-growing companies in Rob's portfolio are almost inevitably doing some sales.

chunks.heading: Marketing as a skill: three layers, and strategy matters most
chunks.text:
- Rob says marketing is not posting on Twitter, and audience building is not a core SaaS skill.
- Marketing has three layers:
  1. Execution: the individual contributor pushing buttons in an ad console or writing SEO content.
  2. Project management: keeping work moving, reviewing it and keeping people accountable.
  3. Strategy: deciding which approaches to test and where to double down.
- Strategy matters most and is the hardest to replace. It can't be outsourced to an agency or handed to ChatGPT.
- He points to 20 B2B SaaS marketing approaches, covered on his channel, on his podcast and in his book *The SaaS Playbook*.

chunks.heading: Four founder archetypes where a missing skill stalls growth
chunks.text:
- **The builder (missing sales and marketing):**
  - This is the most common pattern Rob sees, because he deals with many developers.
  - Technical founders build good products but nobody knows they exist.
  - Builders think the product should sell itself, or that posting on social media counts as marketing.
- **The marketer (missing product):**
  - Typical of info marketers and audience-first founders who move into SaaS. They can drive traffic and sign-ups, but churn is through the roof.
  - In info products, the headline matters and people pay once. If they never use the course, nobody cares.
