  - SaaS needs people who keep using and paying. These founders don't know what to build or how to turn feedback into improvements.
- **The outsourcer (missing development):**
  - Non-technical founders hire an agency or freelancer and expect them to handle both product and development.
  - The top struggle is too many bugs. The next agency, hired after firing the first, wants to rewrite the whole codebase. They ship too slowly and have technical debt by launch, a permanent headwind.
  - Rob believes a developer co-founder or a founding engineer who owns the codebase would make a significantly different business in almost every case.
  - Only about 10-15% of his portfolio companies lack at least one technical co-founder. Craig Hewitt of Castos and a handful of other Tiny Seed companies are exceptions, but the pain is real and ongoing.
- **The vibe coder (a newer archetype, seen over the last 12-18 months):**
  - The product is built with vibe coding, no-code, AI-written code shipped without review, or third-party platforms.
  - Rob has never seen a true seven-figure SaaS built this way. Everyone he has seen or invested in (a handful) needed a rewrite, often at $5-20K MRR when the founder realizes it won't scale.
  - A rewrite means standing still for three, six or nine months, right when a startup's advantage is speed and when it should be responding to the market.
  - His analogy: with tools and lumber but no carpentry skills, you can build an outhouse or tool shed, but a garage, house or skyscraper falls over.
  - Tiny Seed has funded several no-code tools. It now asks up front whether founders are vibe coding or using no-code, and treats it as a meaningful drag on their odds when deciding who gets offers.
  - No-code and vibe coding do get you to an MVP quicker, but there are tradeoffs.

chunks.heading: Three ways to fix a missing skill, in order of preference
chunks.text:
1. **Learn it yourself (preferred, especially for solo founders):**
   - You don't need to master all four, just be good enough to "scrap and get by". The commitment is to take ownership and put in the time to get good at all four.
   - He says the founder is "a jack or Jill of all trades and a master of none. That is the job." Most successful solo founders he has seen did this.
2. **Constrain the idea with the stair-step method:**
   - Pick a business that doesn't need all four skills. A step-one business is a Shopify plugin or a tool built for an app marketplace. MicroConf lists more than 80 of these.
   - Step-one businesses need less development, so no-code or vibe coding can work, like a tool shed or small utility. They have built-in marketplace distribution, so you learn one marketing channel, and they often need no sales.
   - The ceiling is lower, but you stay in the game, build confidence, earn some revenue and learn many skills.
3. **Find a co-founder for a specific gap:**
   - Don't look for a vague "business co-founder". Fill the exact gap in your core four.
   - The most valuable skills in a SaaS are sales and marketing. Their order depends on niche and price point. Don't give away half the company to someone who can't execute in sales and marketing.
   - A non-technical founder strong in sales and marketing needs a developer who also knows product: what to build, in what order, why and how.
   - In his successful portfolio companies the four skills are spread across three co-founders, sometimes two, and occasionally one person has all four. Examples of one-person coverage: Ruben Gomez of SignWell, and Iran Gabrin of Gymdesk (a developer who learned product and then the other two).
   - He points to podcast episodes 807 and 811 of *Startups for the Rest of Us* for more.

chunks.heading: When to delegate each skill
chunks.text:
- The principle: delegate based on repeatability and how standardized and certain a function is, not on a revenue number. Founders should work on the risky, uncertain areas and hand off what becomes repeatable.
- Delegate, don't abdicate: train the person and review their work.
- **Development (earliest and easiest):**
  - A technical founder can hire a developer as early as $10-30K MRR.
  - At Drip, Rob had a contract developer, Derrick, who later became his co-founder. They added a junior dev at about $10-15K MRR. Drip's market (email service providers and marketing automation, with hundreds of competitors) needed years of development just for table stakes.
  - Keep architecture decisions and tech leadership with the founding team much longer. "Delegating execution is very different from delegating direction."
- **Sales (depends on complexity):**
  - A simple, repeatable, one-call close can be delegated at $20-30K MRR. Rob handed off sales at Drip around that range because the calls were similar. His customer success person took over.
  - Enterprise sales (tickets of $35,000 a year and up, with procurement) should be held past $500K, probably into seven figures.
  - With a dual funnel (for example $500 a month and $5,000 a month), hand off the lower-end deals first and keep the high-value ones.
  - If every call is different and complex, you're not ready.
- **Marketing:**
  - Execution (running ads, writing articles, making videos) can be delegated early to contractors and freelancers. It is a black box: it works or it doesn't.
  - Project management can be delegated once you have budget.
  - Strategy is the hardest. The earliest he has seen successful founders bring someone in even to collaborate on strategy is after seven figures, around $1-2M ARR, and it stayed collaborative. At zero-to-one, while you're still finding which channels work, you can't outsource it.
- **Product (usually last):**
  - Typically about $1.5-3M ARR (he says $2-3M to be conservative). He can't think of a single company among the hundreds he's invested in that brought in outside product help earlier.
  - At Drip, he and his co-founder made every product decision until about $5M a year. They didn't have to, but it felt comfortable. Then they brought in a great product person, and it was still a three-person collaboration.
  - Good product people are hard to find and expensive, so the slow-burn approach matters most here.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling lists five decisions from 23 years of bootstrapping: stop consuming and start shipping, embrace boring grindy work, adjust course after mistakes, make increasingly larger but manageable bets, and avoid impulsive decisions in hard times. Each is grounded in his path from an $11k acquisition to HitTail, Drip and MicroConf.

chunks.heading: Stop consuming and start shipping (decision one, 2002)
chunks.text:
- Rob started his first online business 23 years ago. In 2002 he decided to stop reading and start shipping.
- He says many early-stage and aspiring founders are stuck in a "dreamer phase". They read business books, hold a "graveyard of dormant domains", watch YouTube and plan the perfect startup without building anything.
- His own problem was analysis paralysis. He hid behind constant learning.
- His fix was to move from consuming business books to building and launching products.
- He argues there are no secret guarantees of success. "No book, no YouTube channel, no podcast is going to give you the magic secret to guarantee your success."
- Input from people you trust, who have done what you want to do, is still valuable. At some point you have to stop consuming and start shipping.
- Shipping publicly is scary, because of the fear of criticism, judgment and failure. Examples of firsts that feel scary are launching code, publishing a blog post, launching a podcast and recording a YouTube video.
- The more you ship, the easier it gets and the more confidence you build.

chunks.heading: Rank work by business impact, not by passion (decision two)
chunks.text:
- Rob says embracing hard, boring, grindy and scary work "may have been the most important factor in my success".
- His mindset was never to skip a task for lack of passion or interest. He ranked tasks by how much impact he expected them to have on the business.
- He ground out unglamorous work, including:
  - SEO
  - advertising
  - copywriting
  - bug fixes
  - customer support
  - code maintenance and rewriting
- He put in "hundreds and hundreds of hours of tedious, frustrating work" to get things shipped.
- He now does much less work he doesn't want to do. Years of grinding built businesses that give him that choice.
- He credits his background in high school football and track, college track and construction work. He did things he didn't want to do to pay the bills.
- He says to keep hobbies for enjoyment. For a startup, especially in the early bootstrapping period (six months to a few years), "you need progress not passion".
- He calls "I don't want to do that, sounds boring" a huge roadblock. He criticizes founders who only do the fun work, such as posting on X/Twitter and calling it marketing. He says that won't get them there.

chunks.heading: Learn from mistakes and change course (decision three)
chunks.text:
- Working hard doesn't help if it's on the wrong things. Rob had to learn to adjust.
- Lessons he learned, many the hard way, because nobody was saying them in roughly 2002 to 2007:
  - B2C SaaS is not good. After a couple of B2C apps he decided to sell to businesses. Every product he built or acquired after that solved problems for businesses.
  - Low-priced software has higher churn, so he moved toward higher-priced products.
  - Building from scratch takes a long time. Acquiring an app that already has traction and product-market fit gets you there faster. He did a mix of building, launching and acquiring.
- These adjustments grew into what he calls the stairstep method of bootstrapping (described on robwalling.com).
- He says "Failure is only a good thing if you learn from it." Repeating the same mistakes is catastrophic.
- Founders often do the same thing over and over and don't get out of their own way.
- He applies this today at MicroConf and TinySeed. They have tried several marketing approaches. For each one they ask what's working, what's not, why, and how to adjust. They don't "beat our heads against a wall".

chunks.heading: Make increasingly larger but manageably sized bets (decision four)
chunks.text:
- Rob quotes comic artist Dave Kellett: over a career you should make "increasingly larger but still manageably-sized bets".
- His progression of investments:
  - **2005-2006:** about $11,000 on NetInvoice, an acquisition. He saved it by freelancing as a software developer nights and weekends for months, while working a full-time day job with a baby at home. He grew NetInvoice from a few hundred dollars a month in revenue to $3,000-$4,000 a month.
  - **2011:** $30,000 on HitTail, an SEO keyword SaaS tool, funded by the cash from his earlier products.
  - **2012-2013:** almost $200,000 to take Drip from an idea to working software with decent product-market fit. It was funded by revenue from his earlier products and his own grinding, not by wealth or rich contacts.
- He never bet the house. He took on no credit card debt and no second mortgage. He earned the money through freelancing and then products.
- Any single bet could have failed and "would have sucked", but none would have bankrupted him.
- Each step up the staircase can be bigger than the last.

chunks.heading: Avoid impulsive decisions during hard times (decision five)
chunks.text:
- Founders will hit burnout, failure, frustration, money worries about paying bills, and social media criticism. They'll also feel a deep urge to quit or change course dramatically.
- Rob never acted on those emotions in the moment. He calls this a huge win.
- His method is a cooling-off period of at least weeks, sometimes months, to sit with a big decision made while emotionally charged.
- Example: years ago he was frustrated with the startup space, and the team received a seven-figure offer to acquire MicroConf. It felt like they should take it, but they declined. He thinks he would regret selling to this day.
- His principle: don't let temporary emotional states make permanent decisions out of temporary problems.
- He built cumulatively over about 20 years: blog, then books, MicroConf, the podcast, TinySeed and the YouTube channel. Each built on the last. He didn't drop one because it was frustrating at the time.
- His advice is to develop the discipline to weather temporary low periods without making big decisions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling uses Neil Magnuson's $99 to $19 price cut (LTV fell from $683 to $68) to show that low prices attract price-sensitive, high-churn, high-support customers. He argues most founders underprice from fear, and that raising prices within a segment or moving upmarket yields healthier businesses.

chunks.heading: Why cutting price from $99 to $19 backfired (Neil Magnuson example)
chunks.text:
- Rob cites Neil Magnuson, who cut his SaaS price from $99 to $19 a month hoping to grow faster. Churn nearly doubled.
- Customer lifetime fell from 8.8 months at $99 to 3.1 months at $19. Lifetime value fell from $683 to $68, a 10x collapse for the same product.
- Neil's conclusion, which Rob endorses: "cheap prices brought browsers, not operators."
- Replacing 100 customers at $99 with $19 customers at the same revenue takes about 11 times as many customers.
- Rob's experience is that cheaper customers also cost more to support. The $19 business is more expensive to run and makes less money.
- Lower prices can lift sign-ups or trials in the short term. In "almost every case" Rob has seen in 20 years, they make the whole business worse.
- Rob's context: he has invested in more than 240 SaaS companies and has seen this pattern repeatedly.

chunks.heading: Price is a filter: who you attract at low vs. high prices
chunks.text:
- Rob's core claim is that "your price isn't just a number. It's usually a filter." Set it too low and you filter in the wrong customers.
- Low prices attract price-sensitive buyers who want cheap software, not an in-depth solution. They churn as soon as a competitor is a dollar or two cheaper.
- Higher prices attract buyers who have already convinced themselves it is worth it before signing up.
- Higher prices also attract business buyers. A $99 a month tool is a "rounding error" for a business. At $19, many businesses won't take the product seriously and more consumers sign up.
- Rob repeats his advice not to sell to consumers. Businesses mean lower support, higher payments and longer retention.
- At $19, "a lot of people are just going to come along and kick the tires." At $99, the price adds just enough friction that buyers commit more. They onboard properly instead of logging in, poking around and leaving.
- Lower-paying customers are almost always a higher support burden. They are less technical and need hand-holding. A business customer may have a developer or IT person to learn the tool.
- A higher price usually leads to better customers and fewer complaints.

chunks.heading: Underpricing patterns Rob sees at Tiny Seed
chunks.text:
- Rob runs Tiny Seed, a B2B SaaS accelerator. Pricing is one of the first things reviewed at the kickoff retreat, held twice a year.
- Most founders anchor their price too low from day one, often "out of fear, not out of strategy."
- Many anchor to their own cost of doing business instead of the value delivered to the customer.
- They assume a lower price removes friction. Rob says it actually removes "the signal that the product is serious."
- About 80% of incoming batches have some pricing issue. Either the price is too low, or the value metric is wrong. The value metric is the number, such as subscribers or seats, that rises as customers pay more.
- The advice is usually, but not always, to charge more. Higher prices also fund more marketing and sales.
- Across hundreds of Tiny Seed companies, underpricing is "one of the most consistent and correctable problems."
- Raising prices is usually on the table earlier than founders think, and founders who do it are usually glad they did.

chunks.heading: The price ceiling and how rarely founders hit it
chunks.text:
- Rob acknowledges there is usually a ceiling within a particular customer type.
- In his experience almost no founders reach it, because they are too scared to raise their monthly price.
- Of the hundreds of companies he has seen raise prices, he knows of only two, maybe three, that went too high and later dropped them.

chunks.heading: Case study: Jimdo's price increase
chunks.text:
- Rob names Iran Gerpott, founder of Jimdo, as an example of raising prices and changing the business. Jimdo is a mostly bootstrapped company whose only outside money came from Tiny Seed.
- Gerpott raised prices around 2021 or 2022. Rob recalls an increase of between 50% and 100%, though he doesn't remember the exact numbers.
- Gerpott had not raised prices in the previous 5 years. Rob says fear and anxiety, more than the numbers, kept him from doing it.
- After a few calls with Rob, Gerpott raised prices and worked with some existing customers to keep it affordable.
- The change reshaped both the growth trajectory and the churn trajectory of the business.
- Gerpott later sold a majority stake in the company for $32.5 million.
- Rob writes about this in his book *The SaaS Playbook*, which also covers Auren Galperin raising prices for Gymdesk.

chunks.heading: Two paths: raise prices within a segment vs. go upmarket
chunks.text:
Rob says to decide first which move you are making. They are two different moves.

**Path one: raise prices within the current segment**
- This is the same ICP and use case with more money. The increase might be 10%, 30%, or 50% if you are underpriced.
- Every segment has a ceiling. You push toward it, not past it.
- Run it as an experiment:
  - Change the pricing page and leave existing customers alone.
  - Watch conversions for a few weeks or months.
  - If you are sales-led, quote the new price to new prospects first and see how they respond.
  - If the new pricing works and the business is healthier, revisit existing customers later.

**Path two: go upmarket**
- You are changing customers, not just raising prices.
- Rob's example is a podcast tool. A hobbyist pays $25 a month and a business podcaster pays $75. Moving to $500 and $2,000 a month means targeting broadcasters and large podcast studios.
- When you raise prices 10x or 20x, it helps to already have one or two customers in that tier, because their needs differ from your $25 and $75 customers.
- Going upmarket means being more sales-led, and the product may need to evolve in ways you didn't anticipate.
- The payoff is a healthier business with lower churn, higher lifetime value, and more ability to pay for marketing and sales.
- Rob points to a separate video on executing a price increase, including grandfathering existing customers and communicating the change.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling compares free trials and freemium using his 224 investments and a survey of nearly 700 bootstrapped SaaS startups. Requiring a credit card correlates with double the growth and the lowest churn, but he now sees cases for dropping the card early (for feedback) or after about $1M ARR (as a reversible experiment).

chunks.heading: Free trial vs. freemium: the definition and why freemium usually fails
chunks.text:
- Rob defines the difference this way: a free trial ends, either by time ("a 7-day free trial") or by usage (for example, 100 emails through the account). Freemium, which he also calls "forever free," renews automatically. You might get 100 emails every month and only pay when you go over.
- Freemium gives people much less motivation to convert to paid, which is a big reason it is hard to make work.
- In the 2024 State of Independent SaaS Survey, about 29% of bootstrapped and mostly bootstrapped SaaS companies offer freemium. About 51% offer a free trial.
- His default advice is that freemium doesn't work "90, 95% of the time." He suspects many of the 29% freemium offerings are not actually working.
- His data for the survey and for his advice comes from 224 investments and nearly 700 startups surveyed for the State of Independent SaaS Report.

chunks.heading: When freemium might work: Ruben's five requirements
chunks.text:
Rob cites Ruben, founder of SignWell, as one of the most knowledgeable people on SaaS freemium. Ruben's five minimum criteria are:

1. Self-serve with simple onboarding.
2. Customers get to value quickly, without weeks of onboarding.
3. Almost zero cost for each new user.
4. Some element of virality.
5. A very large market, not a small niche.

Rob says that meeting all five still doesn't guarantee freemium will work. These are the minimum criteria he would check before even considering a freemium plan. Generally he tells most founders to avoid it.

chunks.heading: Should the trial require a credit card? Start with who is signing up
chunks.text:
- The key question is whether the person signing up is likely to have a company credit card.
- A software engineer at a very large company might not have one. If that person is your end user, you may not want to require a card.
- Engineering managers are very likely to have a card.
- Rob's Drip experiment: screen one asked for email and password, and screen two asked for a credit card. If someone bailed before entering a card, Drip emailed them about 12 hours to a day later and offered a trial without a card.
  - Roughly 0% of those people became a good long-term fit. There was a trickle, but lead quality was "10 to 20 times worse" than with the card up front.
- Without a card you also get many unqualified people. That can swamp a small team and raise the support burden.

chunks.heading: When to require a card early, and when to drop it early
chunks.text:
- In his last bootstrapped SaaS, Rob required a card up front. He had a launch list of 3,400 people who wanted to try the product, and he didn't want unqualified signups swamping the team. With a big list like that, he would ask for the card early.
- The case for removing it early: you have no brand, only a trickle of visitors, few trial signups, and you need feedback. Letting people in without a card and trying to talk with them can be worth it. He warns you will get a lot of unqualified people and you need to be ready for that.
- His old default was that all founders should ask for a card up front. Now he sees a case for removing it early when you aren't getting enough feedback on the product.

chunks.heading: Experimenting with removing the card once you're established
chunks.text:
- Once the funnel works and you're at roughly $500k, $1M or $2M a year, he suggests experimenting with removing the card, as long as you can roll it back.
- At that stage you have historical numbers and good knowledge of the business, so you can see the impact quickly. It may take a month or two, and you must also look at churn.
- He calls it a worthwhile experiment because it is a big bet, and "sometimes you have to take big bets to really change the trajectory of your business."
- One data point he often thinks about: a company that removed the card after reaching about $1M a year saw absolutely no difference. He notes this doesn't mean the same will hold for your business.
- Check the competitive landscape too. If competitors allow trials without a card, or offer freemium, there is a pull to match them, though that doesn't mean they are making it work. You may need it to win customers.

chunks.heading: What the State of Independent SaaS data shows
chunks.text:
- Share of free trials requiring a card: about 73% in 2020, up in 2021 and 2022, then down by more than 10% in 2024. About three quarters of mostly bootstrapped SaaS companies still require a card.
- Bootstrapped founders require it because it cuts noise and support burden. The downside is that it may turn away a small number of qualified prospects, especially if competitors don't require a card.
- Asia Orangio, founder of Demand Maven, analyzed growth and churn for the report:
  - Month-over-month growth for a trial with a card required is double that of a trial without a card.
  - It is about 40% higher than growth for a freemium plan.
  - Churn is lowest with a card required.
- Rob's read is that requiring a card is the way to go for most mostly bootstrapped SaaS companies. He adds that companies not asking for a card may be earlier-stage, with funnels not yet figured out, which could explain their low growth and high churn.

chunks.heading: The puzzling LTV result and what it implies
chunks.text:
- Orangio also compared customer lifetime value. A free trial without a card showed 2.2 times the lifetime value of a trial with a card. Rob says he "genuinely" can't explain it.
- Free plans had very low LTV. Combined with high churn and weak growth, that makes freemium an uphill battle.
- His hypothesis is that the high LTV for no-card trials comes from later-stage companies with funnels that are more figured out. This fits his advice to test removing the card once you pass about $1M ARR.
- He promotes MicroConf Connect (microconfconnect.com), a paid, vetted community for bootstrapped and mostly bootstrapped SaaS founders.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling argues freemium is really a lead-generation marketing strategy, and that bootstrapped SaaS founders copying VC-funded giants risk delaying revenue and burning resources. He lays out four conditions that must all be present before freemium makes sense, and suggests a 10x price increase as an alternative thought experiment.

chunks.heading: Why Rob calls freemium a marketing strategy, not a pricing strategy
chunks.text:
- Rob says most founders treat freemium as a pricing strategy. He credits Patrick Campbell of ProfitWell as probably the first to see it as a marketing strategy.
- His reasoning: the price is zero, so you earn nothing. Pricing strategy is about value metrics and getting the most from the people who get the most value.
- In his view, freemium is "a way for you to get more leads into your funnel."
- As a default, he believes bootstrappers should generally avoid freemium as a marketing strategy.

chunks.heading: Freemium vs. free trial: the definitions Rob uses
chunks.text:
- **Free trial:** a limit, usually on time (7, 14 or 30 days). It can also be a usage cap in total, such as converting PDFs five times and then the trial ends.
- **Freemium:** he describes it as "forever free," with very limited capacity.
  - PDF converter example: one conversion per month, every month, forever.
  - Email service provider example: up to 100 subscribers on the list, forever free. The trial equivalent would be a 14-day trial or 100 total sends.

chunks.heading: Why bootstrappers shouldn't copy Slack, Figma, Notion, Dropbox
chunks.text:
- Freemium looks like a good default because big venture-funded companies used it well: Slack, Figma, Notion, many no-code tools and Dropbox. It became almost the default for B2C-ish SaaS 10-15 years ago.
- Those companies have hundreds of employees and tens or hundreds of millions of dollars raised, and many are now public.
- A bootstrapper with a team of one to three can't model that. Success depends on when and how you implement freemium, not just on adding it.
- Adopting it only because others did is the real problem.

chunks.heading: The three risks of freemium for a bootstrapper
chunks.text:
1. **It pushes revenue down the line.**
   - Rob cites Dropbox's line that roughly 3% of free users become paying customers within a year.
   - A founder trying to quit their day job and reach $5K-$10K a month can't wait 12 months for 3% of free users to pay. They need willing payers to pay sooner.
2. **It doesn't market itself.**
   - A free plan still has to be marketed.
   - Example: Marie at T.O (a podcast guest) grew to 300,000 users on freemium. She started by sending thousands of cold DMs to get people onto the free plan.
3. **It needs huge volume.**
   - 10,000 free users usually won't get you far. He says you need 50,000, 100,000 or more, depending on conversion rate.
   - Launching a free plan and getting some signups won't produce meaningful revenue quickly.

chunks.heading: Backing out of a free plan, and the 10x pricing thought experiment
chunks.text:
- Rob says you can pull back on freemium after launch. Expect some pushback.
- Two options: remove the free plan from the signup page and grandfather existing free users, or shut it down and make everyone pay.
- His example: in 2011 he acquired an app called HitTail with a free plan that cost a lot in support, headaches and server resources.
  - He shut the free plan down and told users they had to start paying.
  - Of roughly a thousand free users (he recalls "I think it was a thousand"), only a dozen or two dozen stayed on and paid.
  - It was painful and drew many complaints, but it worked.
- When a founder says they want a free plan, he asks the opposite question as a thought experiment: what if you 10x your pricing instead, to lower churn and go upmarket? What would the product have to do to be worth 10x the price? He says this is a useful exercise.
- He discusses freemium at length with Ruben Gomez in episode 725 of Startups for the Rest of Us.

chunks.heading: Four conditions that must hold before bootstrappers use freemium
chunks.text:
Rob borrows these from Ruben Gomez, whom he calls one of the world's experts on freemium for bootstrap founders.

1. Almost zero support needed per customer.
2. Almost zero incremental cost per additional user.
   - Usually fails if free users trigger paid API calls (such as AI requests) or send SMS messages, because it gets expensive.
3. Users can self-onboard and get value from the app very quickly.
4. Some measure of virality or very strong word of mouth.
   - Rob adds that if he didn't have virality, he wouldn't use freemium.

His verdict: with all four in place, the answer is still only "maybe." Without them, he would avoid freemium "at all costs."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling argues pricing is the biggest lever in SaaS and most bootstrapped founders undercharge due to four fears. He shares churn data, the Gather example, and a practical playbook for raising prices, grandfathering, and messaging.

chunks.heading: Why Rob says founders undercharge, and why charge more is still right
chunks.text:
- Rob has called pricing "the biggest lever in SaaS" for years. At early MicroConf events about 13-14 years ago, Patrick McKenzie (patio11) told a room of founders "charge more", and Rob says that advice still holds.
- He points to Sam Altman admitting OpenAI loses money on the $200/month ChatGPT Pro plan. His takeaway is that if a sophisticated tech company can underprice, a small founder can too.
- Pricing is the one thing that, if wrong, can create a terrible business. If right, it can make a business 2, 3, 4 or 5 times more valuable and successful.
- Getting pricing right can be an unfair advantage over competitors.

chunks.heading: The four fears that keep founders from raising prices
chunks.text:
1. **"Nobody will buy if I charge more."** Founders often undercharge while a competitor charges much more, yet still lack the confidence to raise prices.
2. **"My product isn't good enough."** Rob calls this "product impostor syndrome". In almost all cases the product is good enough.
3. **"My competitors charge less."** This is only a real constraint if you are a commodity that can be swapped one for one (a gallon of gas, an orange). The fix is differentiation: features, positioning, focus, brand, or some moat. Otherwise it is "a race to the bottom". He covers this in the SaaS Playbook.
4. **"I might wreck my business."** The odds are low. Rob has seen hundreds, if not thousands, of SaaS companies raise prices. A handful had to roll back, and he has seen a business actually broken only once. In that case competitors dropped their prices and the company didn't follow quickly enough, so the real cause was failing to react to new market data.

Across the 22 B2B SaaS investments he has made, the vast majority were underpriced at some point. The vast majority went "up and to the right" after raising prices. He says you can raise prices too much, but bootstrapped and mostly bootstrapped founders mostly undercharge.

chunks.heading: What raising prices does: faster MRR and lower churn
chunks.text:
- **First-order effect:** more MRR/ARR and faster growth. Rob has shown TinySeed companies that started their batch year in May and raised prices in May or June on his team's advice. Their MRR growth increased significantly, making them "a completely different business".
- **Second-order effect, churn:** he has said for over a decade that lower-paying customers churn faster.
- An anonymous TinySeed company segmented its churn:
  - Customers paying $29/month had net revenue churn of over 11%.
  - Customers paying $99/month and up had net revenue churn of negative 4%.
- Rob says 11% churn "means your business is on fire", and that this one metric can be the difference between a $4 million/year business and one doing $1 million or $1.25 million.

chunks.heading: Case study: Gather's price increase
chunks.text:
- When Gather joined TinySeed, its plans were $39 and $79 per month, and the business was not viable. It couldn't run sales calls at the scale it needed to grow.
- The team encouraged them to raise prices, and they worried they would get fewer customers.
- They moved from $39 to $99 and from $79 to $159. Rob says there was "no difference in conversion".
- Since then they have gone further. Their lowest plan is still $99, the mid plan is $199, and there is a custom pricing plan.
- They lost some solo and more price-sensitive customers, but churn went down and growth accelerated over roughly 6 to 8 months (Rob doesn't remember which).

chunks.heading: Quick tactics for raising prices
chunks.text:
- **Shrink the value metric threshold.** Instead of 3,000 contacts or subscribers for $49, offer 2,500 for $49. This raises the effective price on one or all plans.
- **Drop your lowest plan.** For example, with $19, $49 and $99 plans, start at $49 or $49.99. It is an easy experiment that gets you comfortable without a cheap tier.
- **Don't count on split testing.** Rob has seen approximately zero SaaS companies split test pricing. A few have, but bootstrappers lack the volume, so you take a leap of faith and watch your numbers.
- **Decide whether it is an experiment or a certainty.**
  - If it is an experiment, make it easily reversible and "watch my numbers like a hawk".
  - If it is a certainty, make the increase a marketable event. Email everyone in the trial funnel, non-customers and customers. Try to drive annual conversions ahead of the change by offering to honor current pricing for those who sign up before a set date, even though prices rise in a couple of weeks.

chunks.heading: Existing customers and grandfathering
chunks.text:
- Raising prices for new customers and raising them for existing customers are separate decisions.
- You can change new-customer pricing first, watch it for a month or two or three, and decide later whether to raise existing customers.
- Grandfathering means not raising prices on existing customers. The reasons to consider it are some churn, support complaints and burden, and possible damage to brand or reputation.
- Rob says raising prices on all customers is "usually not always" the right answer, provided you communicate it well.
- Give at least 2 months of notice, but not more than 6.
- **Rob's rule of 15:** if raising prices on existing customers won't grow MRR by at least 15%, it's probably not worth it.
- Never promise to grandfather for life, because in 1, 3 or 5 years you may want to raise prices again. "Never say that anything is for life."

chunks.heading: Structure of a price increase message
chunks.text:
Rob backed this structure out of several well-constructed price increase emails and blog posts:

1. Set the stage.
2. Say "we're changing our pricing".
3. Give a high-level justification.
4. Optionally, give specifics on who is impacted and when.
5. Optionally, give more justification.
6. Close with "please reach out with questions".

He points to Jordan G's price increase blog post for CartHook (viewable in the Wayback Machine) as an example.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling reviewed 192 Tiny Seed revenue graphs and found roughly 85-90% of plateaued companies never broke through. He lays out seven causes (leaky funnel, high churn, not enough leads, competition, tapped-out market, segment-specific PMF, one-time events), rules of thumb to identify each, and founder examples of escaping or avoiding them.

chunks.heading: The SaaS plateau equation: new MRR divided by churn
chunks.text:
- Rob says "churn is the death of SaaS, but churn causes plateaus."
- Formula: a SaaS plateaus at (new MRR added per month) ÷ (monthly revenue churn).
- Example: adding $3,000 of new MRR with 5% monthly revenue churn plateaus at $60k MRR.
- Cutting churn to 2.5% moves that plateau to $120k MRR, about a $1.4M business.
- Unless the fundamentals (new MRR or churn) change, "that's your business. You're going to plateau. Predict it. Avoid it."
- He reviewed the MRR graphs of all 192 Tiny Seed investments and asked founders in Slack what caused each plateau and how they got through it.
- About 85-90% of the companies that plateaued never broke through, so predicting and avoiding a plateau beats hitting one.
- The seven plateaus apply after emerging product-market fit, from roughly $10-30k MRR up into the millions of ARR.
- The solutions are usually obvious. The useful part is diagnosing which plateau you are in.
- The first four plateaus are by far the most common. The last three are rarer.
- The examples he shows are mid-six to seven-figure businesses.

chunks.heading: Plateau 1: Leaky funnel (low-touch trial and signup funnel)
chunks.text:
- Churn is excluded here. A leaky funnel is the path from hearing about you to trial to paid.
- Rob defines it as funnel metrics falling outside his rule-of-thumb ranges for low-touch funnels. The ranges are in the SaaS Playbook (sasplaybook.com/resources).
- If you are within the ranges, the funnel is probably fine. If you are below them, fix the funnel first.
- Example: a credit-card-up-front trial converting trial to paid at 20% is the weakest part of the funnel, and he knows it from experience.
- He defends rules of thumb against critics who call them "common knowledge." They tell you where to look first.
- Fix: troubleshoot the funnel starting at the bottom.
- Example, ScrapingBee (Pierre):
  - They sold a commodity and were 50-100% more expensive than competitors on concurrency.
  - Once new infrastructure let them match price, new customers per month almost doubled "overnight."
  - They kept the nominal plan price and increased what each plan offered.
  - This helped them avoid a plateau as they neared the point where churn equals new MRR.
- Rob calls this a clever way to raise pricing. At Drip he liked the $49.99 and $149 price points, so he lowered the subscriber count per plan twice. That pushed people to upgrade sooner without awkward new prices like $59 and $159.

chunks.heading: Plateau 2: High churn
chunks.text:
- Rob's churn thresholds are in the SaaS Playbook. He means gross revenue churn, not net churn and not logo churn.
- Enterprise or annual-contract companies should sit about two points below the thresholds.
- About 2-3% monthly churn is fine for a non-enterprise company.
- 9% monthly churn is "almost catastrophic."
- Common mistake: founders with 9-10% monthly churn say they "just need more leads."
  - He says "You can't possibly outrun your churn."
  - At that rate you turn over the whole customer base in about eight months, so it is "not a subscription business at all."
  - More leads is the "fix all" people reach for, but it fixes nothing if the fundamentals are broken.
- Fixes depend on why people leave. You can build missing features or checkbox features.
- More often he sees founders stop serving high-churn customers:
  - Low-paying prosumer and B2C-ish customers churn the most and cause the most headaches.
  - Higher-paying customers churn less, sometimes with net negative churn, and are less of a pain.
  - Moving up market often means cancelling your lowest plan, even without raising prices.
- Examples:
  - CartHook (Jordan G): plans started at $49/month and up. He set a $300/month minimum plus a demo with him, and turned away new Shopify stores. Churn was catastrophic, and he wanted a multi-million dollar business. Rob calls this the "velvet rope" policy.
  - Gather: the bottom plan was $29/month when they joined Tiny Seed, with one demo per close. Rob called that not viable. By the end of the season the bottom plan was about $200-250/month, after about 18 months of moving up market.
  - JBoard (Marty):
    - They never hit a plateau, but their analytics predicted an MRR decline from high churn.
    - Trial users split into solopreneurs or wantrepreneurs drawn by low prices, and established businesses that didn't convert because of missing key features.
    - Marty built those features and almost doubled pricing while keeping funnel conversion rates. That avoided the projected decline.

chunks.heading: Plateau 3: Not enough leads
chunks.text:
- Most people jump to this first. Rob lists it third because the cause is usually funnel or churn.
- Diagnose by elimination: if churn is good or great, funnel metrics are within his ranges, and you still aren't growing, you need more leads.
- Leads needed depend on price. $10,000/month software needs far fewer leads than $10-50/month software.
- Example, Flatplan (Kieran), enterprise sales:
  - They plateaued for a long time, perhaps about nine months. Funnel metrics and retention were strong and they closed many deals.
  - Before Tiny Seed they relied on inbound referrals from one large partner and some SEO.
  - The Tiny Seed marketing playbook call used the three-factor framework (speed, cost, scalability) to pick channels. The fast channels (cold outreach, paid clicks) didn't work for them.
  - Kieran: "I accepted it would be a slog." He doubled down on slow, scalable channels: partnerships, organic search, daily LinkedIn posting, a podcast, and recently events.
  - Rob notes you must hold your nerve when tracking is muddy. Kieran is still a bottleneck and is trying to hire a salesperson.
  - Rob: "That is almost the definition of SaaS."

chunks.heading: Plateau 4: Competition and shifting product-market fit
chunks.text:
- Rob has no numbers for this one, only how it feels. You keep hearing "we went with HubSpot because they have a CRM" or "we went with Mailchimp because they're 30% cheaper."
- Product-market fit is a moving target. You can have it and lose it. The product stays the same while the market shifts.
- Example: a Tiny Seed company was growing well until a free open-source competitor arrived. It pulled leads and caused churn, and the founder felt he was losing product-market fit.
- Even a bootstrapped company at $0.5M-1.5M ARR can stop working if a funded competitor undercuts price by half and loses money for years.
- Response: admit what is happening and reposition. Rob points to April Dunford's positioning work and Anthony's MicroConf talk on positioning. Ask how you differentiate, which may mean re-entering the market with a new angle if you have the energy.
- Example, UserList (Benedict):
  - Plateau around 2023, after about six or seven years in the market.
  - Building visual workflows broke the plateau. Benedict's hunch was that it had become a table-stakes feature, and not having it made people dismiss UserList even though its linear campaigns covered most use cases.
  - Rob does not give developers permission to build features randomly: "talk to your customers first."

chunks.heading: Plateaus 5-7: Tapped-out market, one-segment fit, one-time events
chunks.text:
- **5. Tapped-out market.** It is very rare, and usually an excuse to avoid hard work in marketing, sales and product-market fit.
  - Founders often respond by launching a second product or translating the app into Spanish.
  - Senior Place (Jason and JD) serves only single-digit thousands of potential customers and keeps growing.
  - If you have truly tapped out (corroborated by about five people, not founder gut feel), expand horizontally or add verticals. For a realtor product, that means real estate attorneys or mortgage brokers.
  - Postpone.app (Grant): a Reddit scheduler wasn't a seven-or-eight-figure business, so he added Bluesky, Instagram, Threads, Facebook and more. Grant credits breaking the plateau (about six months or more) to a 25% price increase and new platforms, which raised signups and expansion revenue. Users cancelled other scheduling apps to manage all social accounts in one place.
- **6. Strong product-market fit with only one segment.**
  - Blended averages of churn, ARPA and LTV are like a three-star rating that hides a pile of five-star and one-star reviews.
  - Segment customers by industry, lead source and price paid, in a spreadsheet, to find the ICP and the "worst customer profile."
  - Fix: build features to win the weaker segment, or use the velvet rope and stop serving the poor-fit segment, provided the ICP is big enough.
  - He looks at TRM (total reachable market) instead of TAM: how many people per month are switching or newly looking. A $1B TAM with five buyers a month won't grow quickly.
  - Example, Monolith Forensics (Matt Danner): segment A (governments and law enforcement) has high fit. Segment B (private digital forensics labs) plateaus because of missing case and analysis management features. He is building those features and still markets heavily to A.
- **7. One-time events.**
  - Examples: angering your customer base (for instance, raising prices repeatedly and communicating it badly), bad press, a major marketing setback such as Google changes hitting an 80% SEO lead source, or a black swan like COVID.
  - Fix: apologize and fix the problem if you angered customers.
  - During COVID some Tiny Seed applicants doubled monthly while others went to nearly zero.
- Honorable mention is seasonality (Glitch Secure plateaus yearly). He doesn't know a fix, so it isn't on the list.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling argues B2B SaaS is the most repeatable, bootstrappable startup model thanks to recurring revenue, high margins and strong exit multiples. He explains vertical vs horizontal vs orthogonal SaaS, his 2/20/200 validation framework, net negative churn, and why AI is a feature rather than a threat.

chunks.heading: Why Rob thinks B2B SaaS is the best startup business model
chunks.text:
- Rob's core case is recurring revenue. One-off purchases mean "start of the month zero revenue," while with MRR you start each month roughly where you left off, minus churn. This is why businesses push subscriptions for underwear, razors and snack boxes.
- In 2008 he lost 80% of his revenue overnight because his software product was a one-time sale. Recurring revenue does not make a business recession-proof, but it dampens swings. A downturn might cost 20% a month rather than 80% at once, because some customers will not or cannot cancel.
- He says B2B SaaS depends less on luck than most startups. Marketplaces, social networks, medtech and biotech depend on virality, scale or invention. SaaS has a repeatable path: find a problem businesses will pay to solve, validate it, build, iterate and do customer development.
- The risk in SaaS is market risk (will anyone pay?), not "can this be invented?". He says there are only about 20 B2B SaaS marketing approaches (cold email outreach, SEO, content, integrations, events) and you work down the list.
- B2B SaaS is "boring, but much higher likelihood of success" if you follow rules of thumb. He calls it repeatability, not a guarantee, and says "There's no blueprint". He deliberately titled his book *The SaaS Playbook*, not a blueprint.

chunks.heading: Margins, bootstrapping and exit multiples
chunks.text:
- At scale SaaS can reach 80-90% gross margins and 30-50% net margins. Zoom went public with more cash in the bank than it had raised from investors.
- High margin means you do not need venture funding to build one. Rob is an investor in about 220 SaaS companies and sees funding as an accelerant when the unit economics are worked out, but says you have the option to bootstrap.
- Exit multiples are the highest he knows of. Friends selling e-commerce sites get about 2x EBITDA or 1x revenue, and an agency sold for about 1x trailing recurring revenue. In SaaS he has seen 7x topline revenue exits, and a 15x exit on a SaaS doing $3M (a $45M price).
- He says the enterprise value created per dollar of MRR is unmatched, and that the predictability of the revenue is the reason.
- Buyers: as a partner at Discretion Capital (a sell-side M&A firm for B2B SaaS at $2M-$20M ARR), he estimates roughly 70-80% of exits go to private equity and 20-30% to strategics. He says not to quote him on the exact numbers.
- His theory for why PE likes SaaS is uniformity. Churn, lifetime value, ARPA and price points let a buyer judge quality quickly, whereas marketplaces, social networks and medtech have no uniform way to assess health.

chunks.heading: Horizontal vs vertical vs orthogonal SaaS
chunks.text:
- **Horizontal** SaaS can be used by any company in any industry. **Vertical** SaaS targets a specific niche or industry (for example a CRM for construction firms or municipalities).
- **Orthogonal** is a category Rob coined while classifying his portfolio. The product is technically horizontal, but it targets a specific role or title, such as HR directors.
- Knowing who your customer is and where they are is a huge advantage. With a defined role or industry you can cold-outreach the right people and pick the right in-person events.
- Across his 224 investments, horizontal is a minority, roughly 20-30% (he does not know the exact figure). Horizontal companies often grow well, then hit headwinds at roughly $500K-$2M ARR from well-funded competitors. Vertical and orthogonal face less of this.
- Vertical SaaS tends to show lower churn, and often net negative churn once it has traction.
- Why vertical beats a giant like HubSpot for bootstrappers:
  - You build the handful of features that niche wants, in its own terminology, as a pre-configured product.
  - Customers do not have to pay consultants to set up a complex horizontal tool, and you can add onboarding and training services.
  - Marketing and sales cost less because you only talk to one segment.
  - You can often charge a premium. His example is a Microsoft Word license at about $75 versus a specialist Bible-language word processor at $895.
  - Retention is better.
- Rob says venture money mostly flows into horizontal markets. A founder with $100K-$500K or no funding will not have much luck competing head-on with HubSpot.

chunks.heading: Why niching works in B2B but not B2C
chunks.text:
- In B2C you cannot charge much, if anything. It is ad-based or about $4-$5/month, with B2C SaaS around $100/year, so you need huge scale and a narrow niche does not provide it.
- B2B annual contract values in his portfolio run roughly $5,000 to $250,000, so you do not need many customers to build a roughly $5M ARR bootstrapped business.
- High contract values pay for cold outreach (cold DMs, LinkedIn, email). That only works when you know who the customer is, which is why horizontal SaaS cannot do it.
- Even if you know your B2C niche (tall people in Minnesota), you lack the money for outreach.
- He agreed with the host that small differentiation matters more in B2B: a lawn-care CRM that handles seasonality and other industry quirks wins on "they get me", even if 95% of features match a competitor.

chunks.heading: Net negative churn and net revenue retention
chunks.text:
- Revenue churn is the MRR lost in a month divided by MRR at the start of the month. Example: $1,000 lost out of $10,000 is 10% churn.
- Contraction is existing customers shrinking. Expansion is existing customers growing (his example is an email list growing from a $25 to a $50 plan).
- When expansion exceeds gross churn plus contraction, you have net negative churn: with zero new customers, MRR still grows. At 3% net negative churn the business grows 3% a month. The host's equivalent is net revenue retention above 100%.
- It is a minority of SaaS companies that get here. It usually needs pricing on a value metric (seats in a CRM, subscribers in an ESP), very low churn and strong product-market fit. He has seen -12% net churn.
- Buyers weigh it heavily. He has seen similar businesses where one with strong net revenue retention gets 10x ARR, while one with 6% monthly churn gets 3x.

chunks.heading: The 2-20-200 validation framework
chunks.text:
- He says he lands on this approach, though not the only way.
- **2 hours:** research the idea online. Do keyword research in Google, check YouTube, G2 and Capterra, look at competitors and read Reddit complaints. Run it across about 10 ideas to see which have demand, and look for an angle, such as Capterra complaints about competitors.
- **20 hours:** build a landing page with the value proposition found in research (H1, H2, email capture or a booking link such as SavvyCal). Run a smoke test, talk about it in your audience, and do cold outreach on LinkedIn and to your warm network to validate assumptions.
- **200 hours:** build an MVP and get it into users' hands. With AI this might become about 40 hours, and it is not always possible in 200.
- Purpose: many developers build for six months in a basement for something nobody wants, having skipped two hours in Ahrefs and avoided cold outreach. He asks "what are you doing with your life" about developers who fear sales.
- Start with problem-solution fit before product-market fit. The early solution can be virtual assistants in the Philippines collating spreadsheets, or Zapier-style automation, Make or Airtable.
- This is the early module of his course on early-stage B2B SaaS (the 2-20-200 framework is one of 27 modules).
- He learned from Drip (founded 2012, sold 2016) that you must learn your real users even if you are one of them. It was meant for SaaS companies, but bloggers, info-marketers and course creators outgrew the SaaS revenue, so he had to learn how they talk and work.

chunks.heading: AI and SaaS: not dead, five categories
chunks.text:
- Rob rejects "SaaS is dead". He compares it to claims that SEO was dead 15 years ago and that no-code would end SaaS. No-code did have an effect: at Tiny Seed and MicroConf they run 3-4 custom line-of-business apps in Airtable that replaced apps costing $10-15K a year. He estimates no-code took perhaps 15-20% of custom vertical SaaS, not the whole market.
- His brother runs a construction firm and will not build his own software, because it would be buggy, could be hacked, and he does not want to host it. Rob warns about Dunning-Kruger and says the complexity of SaaS is not something AI will solve soon, though he allows that 20 years out is uncertain.
- The host added that maintenance is the hidden cost and that "vibe maintenance" is not a term. Rob agreed, saying AI cannot maintain code yet and that maintenance dwarfs build cost (a rough old figure was $500K to build versus about $3M over 20 years).
- Rob's five categories of AI use in B2B SaaS:
  1. **AI as the core business.** Without AI there is no business (foundation models; fiscal.ai for financial data; Rosie, an AI answering service for service businesses; he is invested in both).
  2. **AI as a feature.** The product survives without it (Notion's writing assistant, Zoom's meeting summaries, Loom's AI titles and chapters). This is the most common in his investments.
  3. **AI for building the product.** Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf, v0. He is not convinced it makes people faster, noting early research that suggests it may not.
  4. **AI for growth.** Marketing and sales (Clay for outbound, Jasper or Copy.ai for content, personalized email, ad optimization).
  5. **AI for operating the business.** Support tickets, resume screening, and checking a hotel or venue contract for non-standard terms, which saved a lawyer round and won concessions.
- Categories 3-5 apply to non-software startups too.
- Investing view: Tiny Seed does not fund many AI-as-core companies because they tend to have high churn and heavy platform risk. They prefer AI as a feature, where there is still a moat without AI and AI helps retention.
- The host's refinement, which Rob liked: don't bolt on a chatbot, and treat AI as an enabler of new features. The best AI features are baked into the workflow and not obviously labeled AI. Rob's example is a portfolio company for real estate buyers' agents that uses AI on listing photos to extract property features not in the listing, so agents can search by them.

chunks.heading: Rob's ecosystem
chunks.text:
- **MicroConf:** education. Free content at youtube.com/microconf, paid mastermind matching, a course on early-stage B2B SaaS, and in-person events twice a year. It has existed for about 10 years.
- **Tiny Seed:** a B2B SaaS accelerator that invests (check sizes of roughly $120-150K) and a paid coaching program for founders above $1M ARR, with one-on-one mentoring and masterminds. He says they raised about $57-58M (he is unsure of the exact figure).
- He has worked in this space for nearly 20 years. Each product came from a need: masterminds, funding, in-person events.
- His podcast is *Startups for the Rest of Us*, approaching 1,000 episodes. His book is *The SaaS Playbook*.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob explains how he stacked tiny niche software products into a living, learned one marketing channel at a time, and why founders should start small, validate before coding, and act without waiting for permission. He also covers hiring developers as a non-technical founder and when funding makes sense.

chunks.heading: Rob's stair-step approach to bootstrapping
chunks.text:
- Rob started with tiny software products in tiny niches, expecting "a couple grand a month, five grand a month". Stacked together, they let him quit his job.
- He had about five or six such products at once. Examples:
  - .NET invoicing software with source code, sold one-time for $300, doing $3-5k/month on SEO and AdWords only.
  - A job board for power line electricians ("linemen") doing about $2k/month.
  - An ebook.
- Together they reached about $10k/month, enough to quit his job and live in California. He later described it as "120k a year" and almost literally the four-hour work week.
- He wrote a long essay called "The Stair-Step Approach to Bootstrapping". The idea is to start small with a single traffic source, then parlay one thing into the next.
- He argues people think too big. Don't read TechCrunch or VentureBeat for this. Ask "how can you get to a thousand dollars a month... five thousand... ten grand a month", which is "way harder than people make it out to be."
- Ideas don't need to be huge. There are thousands, if not tens of thousands, of niche SaaS companies nobody has heard of doing millions a year.
  - Examples he cites: software for analyzing one component of a car, and payroll pension plan software.
  - Friends of his sold tiny-niche companies for tens of millions.
- Rob wants "repeatable small wins, base hits" with a roughly 50/50 chance over time, versus roughly a 1 in 10,000 shot at being Zuckerberg.

chunks.heading: Learning marketing one channel at a time
chunks.text:
- Rob was a developer who learned marketing as a "tool belt". Without marketing or sales you have nothing, and "these things don't sell themselves." Great products with no awareness fail.
- Only about 20-40 marketing approaches work for this kind of software, and you need only a couple to build a good business.
- He learned them one at a time by trial and error, then reused the playbook on each new app:
  - The .NET invoicing product taught him Google AdWords and SEO.
  - He applied AdWords and SEO to the next app, then learned display advertising, then applied all three to the following one.
- His development skills were the superpower because he never had to rely on contractors to maintain, deploy and fix bugs.
- He learned from direct-response books (Dan Kennedy and similar) on copywriting, marketing and sales. He disliked the sleazy parts but kept what was true.
  - "Marketing is just math and human psychology."
  - Math is the funnel. For example, 100 visitors, 5 trials, 20 convert.
  - Psychology means leading with the pain point and benefits, not features.
- Early mistake: he spent about $400 on AdWords before it worked. He learned it isn't "set it and forget it". You must pick keywords carefully and monitor, and be capital efficient without funding.

chunks.heading: What to build first, and who should (not) start a SaaS
chunks.text:
- Rob says not to start with a SaaS app as a first product, even if you're technical. It is "really, really hard," especially without funding.
- Better first products have built-in distribution:
  - WordPress plugin
  - Shopify add-on
  - Course or info product
  - App store listings, where you get discovered
- That lets you focus on code, customer support, deciding features and talking to customers, and learn those skills before building a full SaaS.
- He says a founder needs at least two of three things: technical skills, marketing/sales skills, or funding.
  - Money alone with neither skill will "crash and burn."
  - Money can buy the missing skill. Otherwise learn it, which takes longer but works.
- For non-technical founders, Rob recommends against hiring a single developer. A product role is also needed, and good product people cost over $50k.
  - Better to find a reputable agency that handles product and project management, at a premium.
  - He compares it to remodeling a kitchen: you hire a general contractor with a project management fee rather than six tradespeople.
- Hiring developers is hard for non-technical people. His advice:
  - Go to your network and communities: Indie Hackers, MicroConf (Connect has about 2,000 founders, free), Dynamite Circle, Tropical MBA, Twitter, TinySeed's Slack groups.
  - Ask for recommendations.
  - Reviewing the code is the real hard part after hiring.
  - Bad Upwork stories are common: founders burn $5-10k.

chunks.heading: Buying instead of building
chunks.text:
- Rob had about $10k saved from consulting and realized he'd rather pay $5-10k for an app than spend six months of nights and weekends.
- He paid $11,000 for the .NET invoicing app, which "scared the [expletive] out of me." It was more than he had ever spent on anything, including a car.
- He calls this a "secret" early on: buy things and grow them, skipping the first 18 months of grind to find product-market fit.
- He acquired HitTail in 2011. It was an SEO keyword tool SaaS doing about $1,500/month, with technical problems. He grew it as the only employee, with some contractors.
- He once hired a contractor on Upwork for a ColdFusion app he didn't want to maintain. He preferred Canada or South America for time zones, but today would stay in his own time zone.
- He built Drip (email service provider, similar to Mailchimp) from 2012 and sold it in 2016. From his first launch to the final sale took 11-13 years.

chunks.heading: Validate before you build
chunks.text:
- Rob originally wrote "start marketing the day you start coding". He now regrets that and says to start marketing before coding, through pre-validation.
- Pick a problem that is solved poorly or not at all. Then find people with it and see if they will pay for a solution. This is hard and scary work.
- Ways to find people: cold calls and emails, your network, conferences, Facebook and Slack groups. Example: talk to 20 lawyers, and if none need it, don't build.
- The alternative is to spend $10-15k over six months building, then do the same outreach anyway after launch. Better to do the hard work first.
- Another validation method: check organic keyword search volume for the space (his illustration was something like 50,000 searches a month, which he said was made up).
- Drip validation: he had a small audience from his podcast and blog. He emailed that he was thinking of building it, and about 10 or 11 people committed to trying it and said they'd pay $100/month. He took that as validation.
- On idea theft: he told lots of people his idea and "zero people stole that idea." Execution and marketing are the hard part.

chunks.heading: Funding, TinySeed and "build your business, not your slide deck"
chunks.text:
- Rob never raised money for his own startups. He worked a day job or consulted, then spent 20 hours on nights and weekends. He built one product to $1k/month, used that to buy the next, and so on, until selling Drip.
- "Build your business instead of your slide deck. The best slide deck is revenue." For example, at $10k/month you can raise a round, which a slide deck rarely does.
- Most institutional investors and many angels won't fund pre-revenue ideas, since you've proven nothing until someone pays.
- TinySeed is an accelerator for bootstrapped and "mostly bootstrapped" SaaS founders.
  - First fund: $4.5M, 23 companies, about $120-180k each. A second fund of roughly $26-27M was about to close.
  - It funds people with traction. Applicants arrive from about $1k MRR up to $100k+, with a sweet spot of about $5k/month and up.
  - Advice at the end: don't apply until about $500 to a couple thousand dollars in revenue.
  - Its 42-point checklist comes down to the people, product-market fit and pricing (price sensitivity). He looks for people who ship and don't ask permission.
- He defines "venture funded" as raising roughly $1M+ from institutions, which puts you on the unicorn track of raising every two years and going big or going bust. Angels, small funds and accelerators suit a business aiming for $5-20M a year.

chunks.heading: Execution, velocity and psychology
chunks.text:
- The difference between successful founders and the rest is that they "take action." Examples:
  - One founder writes versus-comparison SEO articles in two days while another takes months.
  - Derek Reimer, his Drip co-founder (now SavvyCal), launches features so fast that velocity alone makes success likely. Not every marketing approach lands, but doing more means half need to work.
- "Most things are speed bumps", not roadblocks. Don't wait for permission from investors, publishers, or a coding skill. Use no-code or do the work manually first (offer SEO manually, for example).
- Patience is undervalued: "11, 12, 13 years" from his first app to his final sale.
- He calls it the "terror of firsts": the first blog post, podcast, book, conference talk. It isn't scary for long, and by the 10th or 50th time you won't feel it.
- His regret: being too risk-averse and too worried about criticism for years. His parting advice: take bigger risks within reason, take action every day, and don't wait for permission.
- He also tells founders to ignore comparison with others and set your own milestones, since managing your own psychology is one of the hardest founder tasks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob Walling interviews Corey Haynes on stair-stepping from info products to a newsletter and membership (Swipe Files, ~$120k/yr). Rob adds advice on marketing to offline niches, buying apps to skip to product-market fit, moving from consulting to products, and international expansion.

chunks.heading: Rob's stair step approach, and how Corey Haynes applied it
chunks.text:
- **Core idea:** Start with one small, simple product, then build on it as experience, revenue and confidence grow. Rob usually describes building a small product in an ecosystem like Shopify, Heroku or WordPress, or buying one.
- **The first steps:** One or two of those small products rarely pay a full-time living. Two or three of them can "buy out my time," which frees you to work on a bootstrapped SaaS.
- **Not only software:** Rob says the early steps can be a book, an ebook, a video course, audio, or an app-store add-on. He has since updated his post to focus on software because he is "all in on SaaS."
- **Corey's path:**
  - Courses: one-time info products
  - Newsletter: free, with a paid archive
  - Community: grouped into one membership
  - Pricing: from $100 to $500 a year
  - Corey calls this "a stair step in action."
- **Rob's reaction:** He called Corey's approach "equally viable" even though it was done "a little differently" from his own software-first version.

chunks.heading: Choosing which SaaS to build: fit with the founder
chunks.text:
- **Personal fit matters most.** Rob says he struggles to answer "what SaaS shouldn't I build," because much of it is personal.
- **Avoid sales-driven companies if you don't want to run one.** Rob says sales-driven orgs "can grow really quickly," but he agrees you shouldn't pick one if it doesn't interest you.
- **Avoid customer groups you aren't fired up about.** He wouldn't launch a SaaS for a group he wasn't excited to work with.
  - He runs Tiny Seed and Microconf because he loves hanging around ambitious founders.
  - Tiny Seed has funded companies selling to home improvement and electrical contractors. Rob was an electrician for a while but has no affinity for that market, and he thinks he would get bored.
- **General cautions:** He mentions "maybe don't go B2C" and that prosumer products tend to have high churn.
- **Staying close to the metal:** Rob sold Drip six years before this episode. He felt himself drifting from deep founder knowledge until he started investing in and advising Tiny Seed companies.
  - He says hands-on gigs like Corey's marketing role at SavvyCal keep your chops up.

chunks.heading: Learning marketing: where to get the skills
chunks.text:
- **Advice for a would-be founder:** Rob says to find a job at a small company with a lot of autonomy.
  - At a Fortune 1000 company you do one narrow thing, such as pay-per-click, in volume.
  - In marketing you would write a lot of content without strategizing or editing it, so you never learn what you like.
- **A hard road for pure coders:** Rob calls learning SaaS marketing "a hard road to go if all you've done is coding to date."
- **Where to learn:** Join Microconf Connect, sign up for Swipe Files, and follow people who know SaaS marketing.
- **Rob's recommendation for developers:** This is the point of the stair step. A developer already has the software skill.
  - Build a Shopify add-on, Heroku add-on, WordPress plugin, or buy a business.
  - You only need to learn enough marketing to rank well in the app store.

chunks.heading: What a developer should build first: app-store add-ons and acquiring
chunks.text:
- **Income range:** App-store add-ons won't become a $5 million business. Rob has seen add-ons reach $10-15k a month, enough to quit a day job.
  - Tiny Seed applicants have been in the $10k-$50k a month range.
  - They aren't venture-backable, and that isn't the goal. The goal is the first two steps, which is "to basically buy out your time."
- **Buying a business:**
  - Rob says he jumped to product-market fit about four times by buying apps.
  - Hitto, his biggest buy at $30k, already had product-market fit. Nobody was marketing it, it was buggy, and its infrastructure was going down about twice a month. He fixed all that, then marketed it.
  - His early acquisitions were NetInvoice and Wedding Toolbox, in 2005-2006. They were in bad shape and he overpaid.
  - NetInvoice cost him $10-11k, "all the money I had in my bank account," which forced him to make it work.
- **Where the gap remains:** Buying a product doesn't solve marketing. If you can't market and sell a SaaS, that gap is still there.
  - Corey notes you can buy your way to product-market fit, but a developer can't "product" their way into growth.
  - Marketers can do this well. Ryan Culp and a partner bought FOMO with seller financing, used profits to pay a developer, and focused on growth.
- **Marketing and building:** Rob agrees software has two full-time jobs, building and selling, and splitting them is hard.

chunks.heading: Moving from consulting to products
chunks.text:
- **Rob's own history:** He was a contractor with a micro agency billing $120-150 an hour. He says working on stuff that made no revenue "killed me."
- **Options he gives a successful consultant:**
  - Acquire a small product to jump ahead.
  - If you have a team, fork one person off to build a product, ideally an app-store product. He calls this "such an easy opportunity these days."
  - If you want to be more ambitious, go after the full SaaS. Then someone still has to market it, and a developer working part-time on the side can't.
- **Corey's additions:** Cut back to part-time consulting, as he did with SavvyCal, or productize the service.
  - Example: content marketing consulting can become a content agency, then an AI copywriting or SEO tool.
- **The income dip:**
  - Moving from full-time work or consulting to products almost always means an income dip, unless you raise funding.
  - It can take two, three or five years to get back to what you earned before.
  - What you gain is "the freedom, you have purpose, you have relationships."
  - Rob's rule: if you optimize for money, keep consulting. If you optimize for lifestyle and recurring product revenue, build the product.

chunks.heading: Marketing to customers who are not online, and expanding internationally
chunks.text:
- **Offline or niche markets (insurance, legal, small theaters, contractors):** Rob lists the options:
  - Cold email, cold calls and cold LinkedIn outreach.
  - In-person trade events, usually a few a year.
  - SEO.
  - Partnerships and business development, which he thinks is underused.
  - Writing for or sponsoring trade publications.
  - Agencies that do marketing or web work for the space.
- **Example:** The Lawyerist is an education brand for lawyers, with courses. Rob knows the founder, lives in Minneapolis, and says legal-software founders know it.
- **Find who has your customers' ear:** Ask who has at least 10 or 20 of your customers on a list. Thousands would be better.
- **Dream 100:** He recommends Chad Holmes's "The Ultimate Sales Machine."
  - Pick your dream 100 customers. For some businesses it is 1,000 or 10,000.
  - Contact them in sequence: call, email, postcard, "lumpy mail" (a calendar in an envelope), then call again.
  - You spend about a year courting them and won't close them all, but they will notice you.
  - It needs the price point to justify it. You need the LTV or ACV.
- **Corey's influence-mapping tips:**
  - Survey existing customers about where they pay attention.
  - Do keyword research in Ahrefs or Ubersuggest.
  - Do video calls with podcasters or content creators in the space.
  - Then pay to play, set up affiliates, create content together, or show up at the conferences.
  - Sometimes there is nothing to map. One Swipe Files member sells to licensed insurance agents in the Northeast, who can be found in state licensing records. DMs, email, postcards and direct mail worked.
- **International expansion:**
  - Rob's advice for a German-language product is to go English next. Spanish is probably the next market after that.
  - Don't launch six languages at once.
  - If an English product is "running out of customers," Rob says don't translate it. "Usually that's the wrong choice." English-speaking markets are plenty big.
  - A translation means the whole marketing site, email support, the knowledge base, sales, landing pages and ads.
  - He can't go on podcasts in Germany because he doesn't speak German.
  - Corey adds that only the largest SaaS companies, such as HubSpot and Salesforce, expand internationally, and that is the last step.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rob hosts Omar Zenholm of Webinar Ninja for an update on bootstrapping a SaaS through COVID growth. Omar does most of the talking; Rob's own contributions are on funding as a tool, finding a way to afford the next hire, and making company values explicit as the team grows.

chunks.heading: Rob's view on bootstrapping vs. funding (Tiny Seed)
chunks.text:
- Rob started Tiny Seed because he "wished I had been able to do this 10 years ago" while grinding on Hitail and Drip.
- Back then he worked a 40-hour day job plus about 20 hours a week of nights and weekends on his products, for years. It was hard to think about quality of life or growth when the question was "can I make the bills this month".
- He says funding is "just a tool": know what you're getting into and use it to grow the business.
- Funding doesn't have to be Tiny Seed. It can be a small raise, or being "mostly bootstrapped".
- He did not assume the guest would say "bootstrap only". He is comfortable with bootstrappers who take bootstrapper-friendly capital.
- He endorses the guest's view that financial breathing room makes it easier to be creative and to think clearly.

chunks.heading: Mission, vision and values must be communicated deliberately as the team grows
chunks.text:
- Rob says many founders start companies partly to avoid mission, vision and values exercises. At past employers they were on a plaque and nobody cared.
- Once a team reaches a certain size, and especially as new people join, you can no longer pass on culture by osmosis. You have to do it deliberately.
- That can be a values statement or any document that captures "this is who we are, this is how we think about things".
- His example is frugality at a self-funded company. If that isn't written down, a hire from a big corporate HQ with a large budget will mismatch with how the company spends.
- He asks where the culture is written down when a company's founders are frugal but a new hire isn't.

chunks.heading: Afford the next hire: "How can I afford it?" instead of "I can't"
chunks.text:
- Rob heard the delegation advice in his first few years of bootstrapping and thought: "this sounds great, but I don't have the budget to hire anybody".
- His answer, to his past self and to anyone thinking this now: ask "how can you afford it?" Carve out the monthly dollars for the next position only, not all the positions.
- Ways to fund that hire:
  - Launch a new product.
  - Increase pricing.
  - Add expansion revenue or premium support.
  - Run an annual special and sell a bunch of annual plans.
- He calls "I can't afford it" a trap: you come up with ideas that solve a problem, then find excuses not to implement them. The fix is to drop the excuse and ask "how can I".
- His reasoning is that the alternative, the founder doing everything, "is not sustainable".

chunks.heading: Founders hit growth "speed bumps", and solving them is the job
chunks.text:
- Rob calls problems like not being able to take a vacation "speed bumps". They feel like roadblocks at the time, and you only meet them if you've grown the company.
- He says much of being an entrepreneur is "troubleshooting and creativity".
- The guest's concrete case: the majority of the team reported to the founders and he could not take a day off. The first fix was an executive assistant who handled admin work, ahead of any big hire. The guest then added a CTO, a head of customer support and a trainer, plus QA through internal promotions.

chunks.heading: Shifting customer base and listening to customers (as discussed with the guest)
chunks.text:
